entries.be10c89b1b9b96a265da7d5c497b063936f236f9: <div sID="gen16091" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="29" osisID="Isa.29" sID="Isa.29"/> <div eID="gen16091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16092" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16093" type="x-p"/> This woe to Ariel, which we have in this chapter, is the same with the "burden of the valley of vision" (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.1">ch. xxii. 1</reference>), and (it is very probable) points at the same event—the besieging of Jerusalem by the Assyrian army, which was cut off there by an angel; yet it is applicable to the destruction of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans, and its last desolations by the Romans. Here is, I. The event itself foretold, that Jerusalem should be greatly distressed, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.1-Isa.29.4">ver. 1-4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">6</reference>), but that their enemies, who distressed them, should be baffled and defeated, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.5">ver. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.7">7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.8">8</reference>. II. A reproof to three sorts of sinners:—1. Those that were stupid, and regardless of the warnings which the prophet gave them, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.9-Isa.29.12">ver. 9-12</reference>. 2. Those that were formal and hypocritical in their religious performances, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.13-Isa.29.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>. 3. Those politicians that atheistically and profanely despised God's providence, and set up their own projects in competition with it, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.15-Isa.29.16">ver. 15, 16</reference>. III. Precious promises of grace and mercy to a distinguished remnant whom God would sanctify, and in whom he would be sanctified, when their enemies and persecutors should be cut off, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.17-Isa.29.24">ver. 17-24</reference>.
entries.3808351bb6134e17a91fc46e5ec0b22a1d2032b1: <div eID="gen16093" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16092" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Punishment of Ariel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 725.)</title> <div sID="gen16094" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Woe to Ariel, to Ariel, the city <hi type="italic">where</hi> David dwelt! add ye year to year; let them kill sacrifices. <hi type="super">2</hi> Yet I will distress Ariel, and there shall be heaviness and sorrow: and it shall be unto me as Ariel. <hi type="super">3</hi> And I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with a mount, and I will raise forts against thee. <hi type="super">4</hi> And thou shalt be brought down, <hi type="italic">and</hi> shalt speak out of the ground, and thy speech shall be low out of the dust, and thy voice shall be, as of one that hath a familiar spirit, out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust. <hi type="super">5</hi> Moreover the multitude of thy strangers shall be like small dust, and the multitude of the terrible ones <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> as chaff that passeth away: yea, it shall be at an instant suddenly. <hi type="super">6</hi> Thou shalt be visited of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts with thunder, and with earthquake, and great noise, with storm and tempest, and the flame of devouring fire. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, even all that fight against her and her munition, and that distress her, shall be as a dream of a night vision. <hi type="super">8</hi> It shall even be as when a hungry <hi type="italic">man</hi> dreameth, and, behold, he eateth; but he awaketh, and his soul is empty: or as when a thirsty man dreameth, and, behold, he drinketh; but he awaketh, and, behold, <hi type="italic">he is</hi> faint, and his soul hath appetite: so shall the multitude of all the nations be, that fight against mount Zion. <div eID="gen16094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16095" type="x-p"/> That it is Jerusalem which is here called <hi type="italic">Ariel</hi> is agreed, for that was the city where David dwelt; that part of it which was called <hi type="italic">Zion</hi> was in a particular manner the city of David, in which both the temple and the palace were. But why it is so called is very uncertain: probably the name and the reason were then well known. Cities, as well as persons, get surnames and nicknames. <hi type="italic">Ariel</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">the lion of God,</hi> or <hi type="italic">the strong lion:</hi> as the lion is king among beasts, so was Jerusalem among the cities, giving law to all about her; it was <hi type="italic">the city of the great King</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.1-Ps.48.2">Ps. xlviii. 1, 2</reference>); it was the head-city of Judah, who is called <hi type="italic">a lion's whelp</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.9">Gen. xlix. 9</reference>) and whose ensign was a lion; and he that is the lion of the tribe of Judah was the glory of it. Jerusalem was a terror sometimes to the neighbouring nations, and, while she was a righteous city, was bold as a lion. Some make <hi type="italic">Ariel</hi> to signify <hi type="italic">the altar of burnt-offerings,</hi> which devoured the beasts offered in sacrifice as the lion does his prey. Woe to that altar in the city where David dwelt; that was destroyed with the temple by the Chaldeans. I rather take it as a woe to Jerusalem, Jerusalem; it is repeated here, as it is <reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Matt. xxiii. 37</reference>, that it might be the more awakening. Here is, <div eID="gen16095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16096" type="x-p"/> I. The distress of Jerusalem foretold. Though Jerusalem be a strong city, as a lion, though a holy city, as a lion of God, yet, if iniquity be found there, woe be to it. It was <hi type="italic">the city where David dwelt;</hi> it was he that brought that to it which was its glory, and which made it a type of the gospel church, and his dwelling in it was typical of Christ's residence in his church. This mentioned as an aggravation of Jerusalem's sin, that in it were set both the testimony of Israel and the <hi type="italic">thrones of the house of David.</hi> 1. Let Jerusalem know that her external performance of religious services will not serve as an exemption from the judgments of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Add year to year;</hi> go on in the road of your annual feasts, let all your males appear there three times a year before the Lord, and none empty, according to the law and custom, and let them never miss any of these solemnities: <hi type="italic">let them kill the sacrifices,</hi> as they used to do; but, as long as their lives are unreformed and their hearts unhumbled, let them not think thus to pacify an offended God and to turn away his wrath." Note, Hypocrites may be found in a constant track of devout exercises, and treading around in them, and with these they may flatter themselves, but can never please God nor make their peace with him. 2. Let her know that God is coming forth against her in displeasure, that she shall be <hi type="italic">visited of the Lord of hosts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">v. 6</reference>); her sins shall be enquired into and punished: God will reckon for them with terrible judgments, with the frightful alarms and rueful desolations of war, which shall be like <hi type="italic">thunder and earthquakes, storms and tempests, and devouring fire,</hi> especially upon the account of the <hi type="italic">great noise.</hi> When a foreign enemy was not in the borders, but in the bowels of their country, roaring and ravaging, and laying all waste (especially such an army as that of the Assyrians, whose commanders being so very insolent, as appears by the conduct of Rabshakeh, the common soldiers, no doubt, were much more rude), they might see the Lord of those hosts visiting them with thunder and storm. Yet, this being here said to be <hi type="italic">a great noise,</hi> perhaps it is intimated that they shall be worse frightened than hurt. Particularly, (1.) Jerusalem shall be besieged, straitly besieged. He does not say, <hi type="italic">I will destroy Ariel,</hi> but I <hi type="italic">will distress Ariel;</hi> and she is <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> brought into distress, that, being thereby awakened to repent and reform, she may not be brought to destruction. <hi type="italic">I will <reference osisRef="Isa.29.3">v. 3</reference>) encamp against thee round about.</hi> It was the enemy's army that encamped against it; but God says that he will do it, for they are his hand, he does it by them. God had often and long, by a host of angels, encamped for them round about them for their protection and deliverance; but now he was <hi type="italic">turned to be their enemy</hi> and fought against them. The siege laid against them was of his laying, and the forts raised against them were of his raising. Note, When men fight against us we must, in them, see God contending with us. (2.) She shall be in grief to see the country laid waste and all the fenced cities of Judah in the enemies' hand: <hi type="italic">There shall be heaviness and sorrow</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.2">v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">mourning and lamentation</hi>—so these two words are sometimes rendered. Those that are most merry and jovial are commonly, when they come to be in distress, most overwhelmed with heaviness and sorrow; their laughter is then turned into mourning. "All Jerusalem <hi type="italic">shall</hi> then <hi type="italic">be unto me as Ariel,</hi> as the altar, with fire upon it and slain victims about it:" so it was when Jerusalem was destroyed by the Chaldeans; and many, no doubt, were slain when it was besieged by the Assyrians. "the whole city shall be an altar, in which sinners, falling by the judgments that are abroad, shall be as victims to divine justice." Or thus:—"<hi type="italic">There shall be heaviness and sorrow;</hi> they shall repent, and reform, and return to God, and then it shall be to me as Ariel. Jerusalem shall be like itself, shall become to me a Jerusalem again, a holy city," <reference osisRef="Isa.1.26">ch. i. 26</reference>. (3.) She shall be humbled, and mortified, and made submissive (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt be brought down</hi> from the height of arrogancy and insolence to which thou hast arrived: the proud looks and the proud language shall be brought down by one humbling providence after another." Those that despise God's judgments shall be humbled by them; for the proudest sinners shall either bend or break before him. They had talked big, had <hi type="italic">lifted up the horn on high,</hi> and had <hi type="italic">spoken with a stiff neck</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.75.5">Ps. lxxv. 5</reference>); but now <hi type="italic">thou shalt speak out of the ground, out of the dust, as one that has a familiar spirit, whispering out of the dust.</hi> This intimates, [1.] That they should be faint and feeble, not able to speak up, nor to say all they would say; but as those who are sick, or whose spirits are ready to fail, their speech shall be low and interrupted. [2.] That they should be fearful, and in consternation, forced to speak low as being afraid lest their enemies should overhear them and take advantage against them. [3.] That they should be tame, and obliged to submit to the conquerors. When Hezekiah submitted to the king of Assyria, saying, <hi type="italic">I have offended, that which thou puttest on me I will bear</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.14">2 Kings xviii. 14</reference>), then his speech was low, out of the dust. God can make those to crouch that have been most daring, and quite dispirit them. <div eID="gen16096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16097" type="x-p"/> II. The destruction of Jerusalem's enemies is foretold, for the comfort of all that were her friends and well-wishers in this distress (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.5">v. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.7">7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt be brought down</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">to speak out of the dust;</hi> so low thou shalt be reduced. <hi type="italic">But</hi>" (so it may be rendered) "<hi type="italic">the multitude of thy strangers and thy terrible ones,</hi> the numerous armies of the enemy, <hi type="italic">shall</hi> themselves <hi type="italic">be like small dust,</hi> not able to speak at all, or as much as whisper, but <hi type="italic">as chaff that passes away.</hi> Thou shalt be abased, but they shall be quite dispersed, smitten and slain after another manner (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.7">ch. xxvii. 7</reference>); they shall pass away, <hi type="italic">yea it shall be in an instant, suddenly:</hi> the enemy shall be surprised with the destruction, and you with the salvation." The army of the Assyrians was by an angel laid dead upon the spot, in an instant, suddenly. Such will be the destruction of the enemies of the gospel Jerusalem. <hi type="italic">In one hour shall their judgment come,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.18.10">Rev. xviii. 10</reference>. Again (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">v. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">"Thou shalt be visited,</hi> or (as it used to be rendered) <hi type="italic">She shall be visited with thunder and a great noise.</hi> Thou shalt be put into a fright which thou shalt soon recover. But (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.7">v. 7</reference>) <hi type="italic">the multitude of the nations that fight against her shall be as a dream of a night-vision;</hi> they and their prosperity and success shall soon vanish past recall." <hi type="italic">The multitude of the nations that fight against Zion shall be as a hungry man who dreams that he eats,</hi> but still is hungry; that is, 1. Whereas they hoped to make a prey of Jerusalem, and to enrich themselves with the plunder of that opulent city, their hopes shall prove vain dreams, with which their fancies may please and sport themselves for a while, but they shall be disappointed. They fancied themselves masters of Jerusalem, but shall never be so. 2. They themselves, and all their pomp, and power, and prosperity, shall vanish like a dream when one awakes, shall be of as little value and as short continuance. <reference osisRef="Ps.73.20">Ps. lxxiii. 20</reference>. He shall <hi type="italic">fly away as a dream</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.20.8">Job xx. 8</reference>. The army of Sennacherib vanished and was gone quickly, though it had filled the country as a dream fills a man's head, especially as a dream of meat fills the head of him that went to bed hungry. Many understand these verses as part of the threatening of wrath, when God comes to distress Jerusalem, and lay siege to her. (1.) The multitude of her friends, whom she relies upon for help shall do her no good; for, though they are terrible ones, they shall be like the small dust, and shall pass away. (2.) The multitude of her enemies shall never think they can do her mischief enough; but, when they have devoured her much, still they shall be but like a man who dreams he eats, hungry, and greedy to devour her more.
entries.b3654a6f2628ce668fc065b46270646a508c6f61: <div eID="gen16097" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings against Judah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 725.)</title> <div sID="gen16098" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> Stay yourselves, and wonder; cry ye out, and cry: they are drunken, but not with wine; they stagger, but not with strong drink. <hi type="super">10</hi> For the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath poured out upon you the spirit of deep sleep, and hath closed your eyes: the prophets and your rulers, the seers hath he covered. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the vision of all is become unto you as the words of a book that is sealed, which <hi type="italic">men</hi> deliver to one that is learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee: and he saith, I cannot; for it <hi type="italic">is</hi> sealed: <hi type="super">12</hi> And the book is delivered to him that is not learned, saying, Read this, I pray thee: and he saith, I am not learned. <hi type="super">13</hi> Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near <hi type="italic">me</hi> with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me, and their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men: <hi type="super">14</hi> Therefore, behold, I will proceed to do a marvellous work among this people, <hi type="italic">even</hi> a marvellous work and a wonder: for the wisdom of their wise <hi type="italic">men</hi> shall perish, and the understanding of their prudent <hi type="italic">men</hi> shall be hid. <hi type="super">15</hi> Woe unto them that seek deep to hide their counsel from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and their works are in the dark, and they say, Who seeth us? and who knoweth us? <hi type="super">16</hi> Surely your turning of things upside down shall be esteemed as the potter's clay: for shall the work say of him that made it, He made me not? or shall the thing framed say of him that framed it, He had no understanding? <div eID="gen16098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16099" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The prophet stands amazed at the stupidity of the greatest part of the Jewish nation. They had Levites, who taught <hi type="italic">the good knowledge of the Lord</hi> and had encouragement from Hezekiah in doing so, <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.22">2 Chron. xxx. 22</reference>. They had prophets, who brought them messages immediately from God, and signified to them what were the causes and what would be the effects of God's displeasure against them. Now, one would think, <hi type="italic">surely this great nation,</hi> that has all the advantages of divine revelation, is <hi type="italic">a wise and understanding people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.6">Deut. iv. 6</reference>. But, alas! it was quite otherwise, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.9">v. 9</reference>. The prophet addresses himself to the sober thinking part of them, calling upon them to be affected with the general carelessness of their neighbours. It may be read, "They delay, they put off, their repentance, but wonder you that they should be so sottish. They sport themselves with their own deceivings; they riot and revel; but do you <hi type="italic">cry out,</hi> lament their folly, cry to God by prayer for them. The more insensible they are of the hand of God gone out against them the more do you lay to heart these things." Note, The security of sinners in their sinful way is just matter of lamentation and wonder to all serious people, who should think themselves concerned to pray for those that do not pray for themselves. But what is the matter? What are we thus to wonder at? 1. We may well wonder that the generality of the people should be so sottish and brutish, and so infatuated, as if they were intoxicated: <hi type="italic">They are drunken, but not with wine</hi> (not with wine only, though with that they were often drunk), and they <hi type="italic">erred through wine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.28.7">ch. xxviii. 7</reference>. They were drunk with the love of pleasures, with prejudices against religion, and with the corrupt principles they had imbibed. Like drunken men, they know not what they do or say, nor whither they go. They are not sensible of the divine rebukes they are under. <hi type="italic">They have beaten me, and I felt it not,</hi> says the drunkard, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.35">Prov. xxiii. 35</reference>. God speaks to them once, yea, twice; but, like men drunk, they perceive it not, they understand it not, but forget the law. <hi type="italic">They stagger</hi> in their counsels, are unstable and unsteady, and stumble at every thing that lies in their way. There is such a thing as spiritual drunkenness. 2. It is yet more strange that God himself should have <hi type="italic">poured out upon them a spirit of deep sleep, and closed their eyes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.10">v. 10</reference>), that he who bids them awake and open their eyes should yet lay them to sleep and shut their eyes; but it is in away of righteous judgment, to punish them for their <hi type="italic">loving darkness rather than light,</hi> their loving sleep. When God by his prophets called them they said, <hi type="italic">Yet a little sleep, a little slumber;</hi> and therefore he gave them up to strong delusions, and said, <hi type="italic">Sleep on now.</hi> This is applied to the unbelieving Jews, who rejected the gospel of Christ, and were justly hardened in their infidelity, till wrath came upon them to the uttermost. <reference osisRef="Rom.11.8">Rom. xi. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">God has given them the spirit of slumber.</hi> And we have reason to fear it is the woeful case of many who live in the midst of gospel light. 3. It is very sad that this should be the case with those who were their prophets, and rulers, and seers, that those who should have been their guides were themselves blindfolded; and it is easy to tell what the fatal consequences will be when the blind lead the blind. This was fulfilled when, in the latter days of the Jewish church, the chief priests, and the scribes, and the elders of the people, were the great opposers of Christ and his gospel, and brought themselves under a judicial infatuation. 4. The sad effect of this was that all the means of conviction, knowledge, and grace, which they enjoyed, were ineffectual, and did not answer the end (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.11-Isa.29.12">v. 11, 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The vision of all the</hi> prophets, true and false, <hi type="italic">has become to you as the words of a book,</hi> or letter, <hi type="italic">that is sealed up;</hi> you cannot discern the truth of the real visions and the falsehood of the pretended ones." Or, every vision particularly that this prophet had seen for them, and published to them, had become unintelligible; they had it among them, but were never the wiser for it, any more than a man (though a good scholar) is for a book delivered to him sealed up, and which he must not open the seals of. He sees it is a book, and that is all; he knows nothing of what is in it. So they knew that what Isaiah said was a vision and prophecy, but the meaning of it was hidden from them; it was only a sound of words to them, which they were not at all alarmed by, nor affected with; it answered not the intention, for it made no impression at all upon them. Neither the learned nor the unlearned were the better for all the messages God sent them by his servants the prophets, nor desired to be so. The ordinary sort of people excused themselves from regarding what the prophets said with their want of learning and a liberal education, as if they were not concerned to know and do the will of God because they were not bred scholars: <hi type="italic">It is nothing to me, I am not learned.</hi> Those of better rank pretended that the prophet had a peculiar way of speaking, which was obscure to them, and which, though they were men of letters, they had not been used to; and, <hi type="italic">Si non vis intelligi, debes negligi—If you wish not to be understood, you deserve to be neglected.</hi> Both these are groundless pretences; for God's prophets have been no unfaithful debtors either to the wise or to the unwise, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.14">Rom. i. 14</reference>. Or we may take it thus:—The book of prophecy was given to them sealed, so that they could not read it, as a just judgment upon them; because it had often been delivered to them unsealed, and they would not take pains to learn the language of it, and then made excuse for their not reading it because they were not learned. But observe, "The vision has become thus to you whose minds the god of this world has blinded; but it is not so in itself, it is not so to all; the same vision which to you is a <hi type="italic">savour of death unto death</hi> to others is and shall be a <hi type="italic">savour of life unto life.</hi>" Knowledge is easy to him that understands. <div eID="gen16099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16100" type="x-p"/> II. The prophet, in God's name, threatens those that were formal and hypocritical in their exercises of devotion, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.13-Isa.29.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen16100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16101" type="x-p"/> 1. The sin that is here charged upon them—dissembling with God in their religious performances, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.13">v. 13</reference>. He that knows the heart, and cannot be imposed upon with shows and pretences, charges it upon them, whether their hearts condemn them for it or no. He that is greater than the heart, and knows all things, knows that though they <hi type="italic">draw nigh to him with their mouth,</hi> and <hi type="italic">honour him with their lips,</hi> yet they are not sincere worshippers. To worship God is to make our approaches to him, and to present our adorations of him; it is to draw nigh to him as those that have business with him, with an intention therein to honour him. This we are to do with our mouth and our lips, in speaking of him and in speaking to him; we must <hi type="italic">render to him the calves of our lips,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.14.2">Hosea xiv. 2</reference>. And, if the heart be full of his love and fear, out of the abundance of that the mouth will speak. But there are many whose religion is lip-labour only. They say that which expresses an approach to God and an adoration of him, but it is only from the teeth outward. For, (1.) They do not apply their minds to the service. When they pretend to be speaking to God they are thinking of a thousand impertinences: <hi type="italic">The have removed their hearts far from me,</hi> that they might not be employed in prayer, nor come within reach of the word. When work was to be done for God, which required the heart, that was sent out of the way on purpose, with the fool's eyes, into the ends of the earth. (2.) They do not make the word of God the rule of their worship, nor his will their reason: <hi type="italic">Their fear towards me is taught by the precept of men.</hi> They worshipped the God of Israel, not according to his appointment, but their own inventions, the directions of their false prophets or their idolatrous kings, or the usages of the nations that were round about them. The tradition of the elders was of more value and validity with them than the laws which God commanded Moses. Or, if they did worship God in a way conformable to his institution in the days of Hezekiah, a great reformer, they had more an eye to the precept of the king than to God's command. This our Saviour applies to the Jews in his time, who were formal in their devotions and wedded to their own inventions, and pronounces concerning them that in vain they did worship God, <reference osisRef="Matt.15.8-Matt.15.9">Matt. xv. 8, 9</reference>. <div eID="gen16101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16102" type="x-p"/> 2. It is a spiritual judgment with which God threatens to punish them for their spiritual wickedness (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will proceed to do a marvellous work.</hi> They did one strange thing; they removed all sincerity from their hearts. Now God will go on and do another; he will remove all sagacity from their heads. <hi type="italic">The wisdom of their wise men shall perish.</hi> They played the hypocrite, and thought to put a cheat upon God, and now they are left to themselves to play the fool, and not only to put a cheat upon themselves, but to be easily cheated by all about them. Those that make religion no more than a pretence, to serve a turn, are out in their politics; and it is just with God to deprive those of their understanding who part with their uprightness. This was fulfilled in the wretched infatuation which the Jewish nation were manifestly under, after they had rejected the gospel of Christ; they removed their hearts far from God, and therefore God justly removed wisdom far from them, and hid from their eyes the things that belonged even to their temporal peace. This is a marvelous work; it is surprising, it is astonishing, that wise men should of a sudden lose their wisdom and be given up to strong delusions. Judgments on the mind, though least taken notice of, are to be most wondered at. <div eID="gen16102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16103" type="x-p"/> III. He shows the folly of those that though to act separately and secretly from God, and were carrying on designs independent upon God and which they projected to conceal from his all-seeing eye. Here we have, 1. Their politics described (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.15">v. 15</reference>): They <hi type="italic">seek deep to hide their counsel from the Lord,</hi> that he may not know either what they do or what they design; they say, "Who sees us? No man, and therefore not God himself." The consultations they had about their own safety they kept to themselves, and never asked God's advice concerning them; nay, they knew they were displeasing to him, but thought they could conceal them from him; and, if he did not know them, he could not baffle and defeat them. See what foolish fruitless pains sinners take in their sinful ways; they seek deep, they sink deep, to hide their counsel from the Lord, who sits in heaven and laughs at them. Note, A practical disbelief of God's omniscience is at the bottom both of the carnal worships and of the carnal confidences of hypocrites; <reference osisRef="Ps.94.7">Ps. xciv. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.12">Ezek. viii. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.9">ix. 9</reference>. 2. The absurdity of their politics demonstrated (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.16">v. 16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Surely your turning of things upside down</hi> thus, your various projects, turning your affairs this and that way to make them shape as you would have them—or rather your inverting the order of things, and thinking to make God's providence give attendance to your projects, and that God must know no more than you think fit, which is perfectly turning things upside down and beginning at the wrong end—<hi type="italic">shall be esteemed as the potter's clay.</hi> God will turn and manage you, and all your counsels, with as much ease and as absolute a power as the potter forms and fashions his clay." See how God despises, and therefore what little reason we have to dread, those contrivances of men that are carried on without God, particularly those against him. (1.) Those that think to hide their counsels from God do in effect deny him to be their Creator. It is as if the work should say of him that made it, "He made me not; I made myself." If God made us, he certainly knows us as the Psalmist shows, (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.1">Ps. cxxxix. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.13-Ps.139.16">13-16</reference>); so that those who say that he does not see them might as well say that he did not make them. Much of the wickedness of the wicked arises from this, they forget that God formed them, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.18">Deut. xxxii. 18</reference>. Or, (2.) Which comes to the same thing, they deny him to be a wise Creator: <hi type="italic">The thing framed saith of him that framed it, He had no understanding;</hi> for if he had understanding to make us so curiously, especially to make us intelligent beings and to <hi type="italic">put understanding into the inward part</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.38.36">Job xxxviii. 36</reference>), no doubt he has understanding to know us and all we say and do. As those that quarrel with God, so those that think to conceal themselves from him, do in effect charge him with folly; but <hi type="italic">he that formed the eye, shall he not see?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.94.9">Ps. xciv. 9</reference>.
entries.5beb73efafeb6cd45d6f980642cdd75037cf2d4f: <div eID="gen16103" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Promises to Israel; Character of Persecutors; Promises of Jacob. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 725.)</title> <div sID="gen16104" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> <hi type="italic">Is</hi> it not yet a very little while, and Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field, and the fruitful field shall be esteemed as a forest? <hi type="super">18</hi> And in that day shall the deaf hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind shall see out of obscurity, and out of darkness. <hi type="super">19</hi> The meek also shall increase <hi type="italic">their</hi> joy in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the poor among men shall rejoice in the Holy One of Israel. <hi type="super">20</hi> For the terrible one is brought to nought, and the scorner is consumed, and all that watch for iniquity are cut off: <hi type="super">21</hi> That make a man an offender for a word, and lay a snare for him that reproveth in the gate, and turn aside the just for a thing of nought. <hi type="super">22</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob, Jacob shall not now be ashamed, neither shall his face now wax pale. <hi type="super">23</hi> But when he seeth his children, the work of mine hands, in the midst of him, they shall sanctify my name, and sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and shall fear the God of Israel. <hi type="super">24</hi> They also that erred in spirit shall come to understanding, and they that murmured shall learn doctrine. <div eID="gen16104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16105" type="x-p"/> Those that thought to hide their counsels from the Lord were said to turn things upside down (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.16">v. 16</reference>), and they intended to do it unknown to God; but God here tells them that he will turn things upside down his way; and let us see whose word shall stand, his or theirs. They disbelieve Providence: "Wait awhile," says God, "and you shall be convinced by ocular demonstration that there is a God who governs the world, and that he governs it and orders all the changes that are in it for the good of his church." The wonderful revolution here foretold may refer primarily to the happy settlement of the affairs of Judah and Jerusalem after the defeat of Sennacherib's attempt, and the repose which good people then enjoyed, when they were delivered from the alarms of the sword both of war and persecution. But it may look further, to the rejection of the Jews at the first planting of the gospel (for their hypocrisy and infidelity were here foretold, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.13">v. 13</reference>) and the admission of the Gentiles into the church. <div eID="gen16105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16106" type="x-p"/> I. In general, it is a great and surprising change that is here foretold, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.17">v. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">Lebanon,</hi> that was a forest, <hi type="italic">shall be turned into a fruitful field;</hi> and Carmel, that was a fruitful field, shall become a forest. It is a counterchange. Note, Great changes, both for the better and for the worse, are often made in a very little while. It was a sign given them of the defeat of Sennacherib that the ground should be more than ordinarily fruitful (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.30">ch. xxxvii. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">You shall eat this year such as grows of itself;</hi> food for man shall be (as food for beasts is) the spontaneous product of the soil. Then Lebanon became a fruitful field, so fruitful that that which used to be reckoned a fruitful field in comparison with it was looked upon but as a forest. When a great harvest of souls was gathered in to Christ from among the Gentiles then the wilderness was turned into a fruitful field; and the Jewish church, that had long been a fruitful field, became a desolate and deserted forest, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">ch. liv. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen16106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16107" type="x-p"/> II. In particular, <div eID="gen16107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16108" type="x-p"/> 1. Those that were ignorant shall become intelligent, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.18">v. 18</reference>. Those that understood not this prophecy (but it was to them as a sealed book, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.11">v. 11</reference>) shall, when it is accomplished, understand it, and shall acknowledge, not only the hand of God in the event, but the voice of God in the prediction of it: <hi type="italic">The deaf shall then hear the words of the book.</hi> The fulfilling of prophecy is the best exposition of it. The poor Gentiles shall then have divine revelation brought among them; and those that sat in darkness shall see a great light, those that were blind shall see out of obscurity; for the gospel was sent to them to <hi type="italic">open their eyes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.26.18">Acts xxvi. 18</reference>. Observe, In order to the making of men fruitful in good affections and actions, the course God's grace takes with them is to open their understandings and make them hear the words of God's book. <div eID="gen16108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16109" type="x-p"/> 2. Those that were erroneous shall become orthodox (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.24">v. 24</reference>): <hi type="italic">Those that erred in spirit,</hi> that were under mistakes and misapprehensions concerning the words of the book and the meaning of them, shall come to understanding, to a right understanding of things; the Spirit of truth shall rectify their mistakes and lead them into all truth. This should encourage us to pray for <hi type="italic">those that have erred and are deceived,</hi> that God can, and often does, bring such to understanding. Those that murmured at the truths of God as hard sayings, and loved to pick quarrels with them, shall learn the true meaning of these doctrines, and then they will be better reconciled to them. Those that erred concerning the providence of God as to public affairs, and murmured at the disposals of it, when they shall see the issue of things shall better understand them and be aware of what God was designing in all, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.9">Hos. xiv. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen16109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16110" type="x-p"/> 3. Those that were melancholy shall become cheerful and pleasant (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">The meek also shall increase their joy in the Lord.</hi> Those who are poor in the world and poor in spirit, who, being in affliction, accommodate themselves to their affliction, are purely passive and not passionate, when they see God appearing for them, they shall <hi type="italic">add,</hi> or <hi type="italic">repeat, joy in the Lord.</hi> This intimates that even in their distress they kept up their joy in the Lord, but now they increased it. Note, Those who, when they are in trouble, can truly rejoice in God, shall soon have cause given them greatly to rejoice in him. When joy in the world is decreasing and fading joy in God is increasing and getting round. This shining light shall shine more and more; for that which is aimed at is that <hi type="italic">this joy may be full.</hi> Even <hi type="italic">the poor among men</hi> may rejoice in the Holy One of Israel, and their poverty needs not deprive them of that joy, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.17-Hab.3.18">Hab. iii. 17, 18</reference>. And the meek, the humble, the patient, and dispassionate, shall grow in this joy. Note, The grace of meekness will contribute very much to the increase of our holy joy. <div eID="gen16110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16111" type="x-p"/> 4. The enemies, that were formidable, shall become despicable. Sennacherib, that <hi type="italic">terrible one,</hi> and his great army, that put the country into such a consternation, shall be <hi type="italic">brought to nought</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.20">v. 20</reference>), shall be quite disabled to do any further mischief. The power of Satan, that terrible one indeed, shall be broken by the prevalency of Christ's gospel; and those that were subject to bondage through fear of him that had the power of death shall be delivered, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.14-Heb.2.15">Heb. ii. 14, 15</reference>. <div eID="gen16111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16112" type="x-p"/> 5. The persecutors, that were vexatious, shall be quieted, and so those they were troublesome to shall be quiet from the fear of them. To complete the repose of God's people, not only the terrible one from abroad shall be brought to nought, but the scorners at home too shall be consumed and cut off by Hezekiah's reformation. Those are a happy people, and likely to be so, who, when God gives them victory and success against their terrible enemies abroad, take care to suppress vice, and profaneness, and the spirit of persecution, those more dangerous enemies at home. Or, They shall be consumed and cut off by the judgments of God, shall be singled out to be made examples of. Or, They shall insensibly waste away, being put to confusion by the fulfilling of those predictions which they had made a jest of. Observe what had been the wickedness of these scorners, for which they should be cut off. They had been persecutors of God's people and prophets, probably of the prophet Isaiah particularly, and therefore he complains thus feelingly of them and of their subtle malice. Some as informers and persecutors, others as judges, did all they could to take away his life, or at least his liberty. And this is very applicable to the chief priests and Pharisees, who persecuted Christ and his apostles, and for that sin they and their nation of scorners were cut off and consumed. (1.) They ridiculed the prophets and the serious professors of religion; they despised them, and did their utmost to bring them into contempt; they were scorners, and sat in the seat of the scornful. (2.) They lay in wait for an occasion against them. By their spies they <hi type="italic">watch for iniquity,</hi> to see if they can lay hold of any thing that is said or done that may be called an iniquity. Or they themselves watch for an opportunity to do mischief, as Judas did to betray our Lord Jesus. (3.) They took advantage against them for the least slip of the tongue; and, if a thing were ever so little said amiss, it served them to ground an indictment upon. They <hi type="italic">made a man,</hi> though he were ever so wise and good a man, though he were a man of God, <hi type="italic">an offender for a word,</hi> a word mischosen or misplaced, when they could not but know that it was well meant, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.21">v. 21</reference>. They cavilled at every word that the prophets spoke to them by way of admonition, though ever so innocently spoken, and without any design to affront them. They put the worst construction upon what was said, and made it criminal by strained innuendoes. Those who consider how apt we all are to speak unadvisedly, and to mistake what we hear, will think it very unjust and unfair to <hi type="italic">make a man an offender for a word.</hi> (4.) They did all they could to bring those into trouble that dealt faithfully with them and told them of their faults. Those that <hi type="italic">reprove in the gates,</hi> reprovers by office, that were bound by the duty of their place, as prophets, as judges, and magistrates, to show people their transgressions, they hated these, and laid snares for them, as the Pharisees' emissaries, who were sent to watch our Saviour that they might <hi type="italic">entangle him in his talk</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.15">Matt. xxii. 15</reference>), that they might have something to lay to his charge which might render him odious to the people or obnoxious to the government. <hi type="italic">So persecuted they the prophets;</hi> and it is next to impossible for the most cautious to place their words so warily as to escape such snares. See how base wicked people are, who bear ill-will to those who, out of good-will to them, seek to save their souls from death; and see what need reprovers have both of courage to do their duty and of prudence to avoid the snare. (5.) They pervert judgment, and will never let an honest man carry an honest cause: <hi type="italic">They turn aside the just for a thing of nought;</hi> they condemn him, or give the cause against him, upon no evidence, no colour or pretence whatsoever. They run a man down, and misrepresent him, by all the little arts and tricks they can devise, as they did our Saviour. We must not think it strange if we see the best of men thus treated; <hi type="italic">the disciple is not greater than his Master.</hi> But wait awhile, and God will not only <hi type="italic">bring forth their righteousness,</hi> but cut off and consume these scorners. <div eID="gen16112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16113" type="x-p"/> 6. Jacob, who was made to blush by the reproaches, and made to tremble by the threatenings, of his enemies, shall now be relieved both against his shame and against his fear, by the rolling away of those reproaches and the defeating of those threatenings (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.22">v. 22</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thus the Lord saith who redeemed Abraham,</hi> that is, called him out of Ur of the Chaldees, and so rescued him from the idolatry of his fathers and plucked him as a <hi type="italic">brand out of the fire.</hi> He that redeemed Abraham out of his snares and troubles will redeem all that are by faith his genuine seed out of theirs. He that began his care of his church in the redemption of Abraham, when it and its Redeemer were in his loins, will not now cast off the care of it. Because the enemies of his people are so industrious both to blacken them and to frighten them, therefore he will appear for the house of Jacob, and they shall not be ashamed as they have been, but shall have wherewith to answer those that reproach them, nor shall <hi type="italic">their faces now wax pale;</hi> but they shall gather courage, and look their enemies in the face without change of countenance, as those have reason to do who have the God of Abraham on their side. <div eID="gen16113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16114" type="x-p"/> 7. Jacob, who thought his family would be extinct and the entail of religion quite cut off, shall have the satisfaction of seeing a numerous progeny devoted to God for a generation, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.23">v. 23</reference>. (1.) He shall see his children, multitudes of believers and praying people, the spiritual seed of faithful Abraham and wrestling Jacob. Having his quiver full of these arrows, he <hi type="italic">shall not be ashamed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.22">v. 22</reference>) but shall speak with his enemy in the gate, <reference osisRef="Ps.127.5">Ps. cxxvii. 5</reference>. Christ shall <hi type="italic">not be ashamed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.7">ch. l. 7</reference>), for <hi type="italic">he shall see his seed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">ch. liii. 10</reference>); he sees some, and foresees more, <hi type="italic">in the midst of him,</hi> flocking to the church, and residing there. (2.) His children are the work of God's hands; being formed by him, they are formed for him, his <hi type="italic">workmanship, created unto good works.</hi> It is some comfort to parents to think that their children are God's creatures, the work of the hands of his grace. (3.) He and his children shall sanctify the name of God as their God, as <hi type="italic">the Holy One of Jacob,</hi> and shall fear and worship the God of Israel. This is opposed to his being ashamed and waxing pale; when he is delivered from his contempts and dangers he shall not magnify himself, but <hi type="italic">sanctify the Holy One of Jacob.</hi> If God make our condition easy, we must endeavour to make his name glorious. Parents and children are ornaments and comforts indeed to each other when they join in sanctifying the name of God. When parents give up their children, and children give up themselves, to God, to be <hi type="italic">to him for a name and a praise,</hi> then the forest will soon become a fruitful field.  <chapter eID="Isa.29"/> <div eID="gen16114" type="x-p"/>

entries.28922b22049469b0f47899540078d63e4f9dc5c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8830"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 29</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.29.1-Isa.29.24">Is 29:1-24</reference>. Coming Invasion of Jerusalem: Its Failure: Unbelief of the Jews.</title> <div sID="gen14720" type="x-p"/> This chapter opens the series of prophecies as to the invasion of Judea under Sennacherib, and its deliverance.<div eID="gen14720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14721" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8830"/><hi type="bold">1. Ariel--</hi>Jerusalem; Ariel means "Lion of God," that is, city rendered by God invincible: the lion is emblem of a mighty hero (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.20">2Sa 23:20</reference>). Otherwise "Hearth of God," that is, place where the altar-fire continually burns to God (<reference osisRef="Isa.31.9">Is 31:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.15">Eze 43:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen14721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14722" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">add ... year to year--</hi>ironically; suffer one year after another to glide on in the round of formal, heartless "sacrifices." Rather, "add yet another year" to the one just closed [Maurer]. Let a year elapse and a little more (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.10">Is 32:10</reference>, Margin).<div eID="gen14722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14723" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">let ... kill sacrifices--</hi>rather, "let the beasts (of another year) go round" [Maurer]; that is, after the completion of a year "I will distress Ariel." <div eID="gen14723" type="x-p"/>
entries.6eec22a5e9771a444b4b54384491c136dfeaf029: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8831"/><div sID="gen14724" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8831"/><hi type="bold">2. Yet--</hi>rather, "Then."<div eID="gen14724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14725" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heaviness ... sorrow--</hi>rather, preserving the Hebrew paronomasia, "groaning" and "moaning."<div eID="gen14725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14726" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as Ariel--</hi>either, "the city shall be as a lion of God," that is, it shall emerge from its dangers unvanquished; or "it shall be as the altar of burnt offering," consuming with fire the besiegers (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.6">Is 29:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.30">Is 30:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.31.9">31:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.10.2">Le 10:2</reference>); or best, as <reference osisRef="Isa.29.3">Is 29:3</reference> continues the threat, and the promise of deliverance does not come till <reference osisRef="Isa.29.4">Is 29:4</reference>, "it shall be like a hearth of burning," that is, a scene of devastation by fire [G. V. Smith]. The prophecy, probably, contemplates ultimately, besides the affliction and deliverance in Sennacherib's time, the destruction of Jerusalem by Rome, the dispersion of the Jews, their restoration, the destruction of the enemies that besiege the city (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.2">Zec 14:2</reference>), and the final glory of Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.17-Isa.29.24">Is 29:17-24</reference>). <div eID="gen14726" type="x-p"/>
entries.e77dfc734f5846972fb26e10ce0677a8085d65e5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8832"/><div sID="gen14727" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8832"/><hi type="bold">3. I--</hi>Jehovah, acting through the Assyrian, &c., His instruments (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.5">Is 10:5</reference>).<div eID="gen14727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14728" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mount--</hi>an artificial mound formed to out-top high walls (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.33">Is 37:33</reference>); else a station, namely, of warriors, for the siege.<div eID="gen14728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14729" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">round about--</hi>not fully realized under Sennacherib, but in the Roman siege (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.43">Lu 19:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.21.20">21:20</reference>).<div eID="gen14729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14730" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forts--</hi>siege-towers (<reference osisRef="Deut.20.20">De 20:20</reference>). <div eID="gen14730" type="x-p"/>
entries.32b8a2e4ef0e932fe1a50d9cc21efe6ed47e0e79: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8833"/><div sID="gen14731" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8833"/>4. Jerusalem shall be as a captive, humbled to the dust. Her voice shall come from the earth as that of the spirit-charmers or necromancers (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">Is 8:19</reference>), faint and shrill, as the voice of the dead was supposed to be. Ventriloquism was doubtless the trick caused to make the voice appear to come from the earth (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.3">Is 19:3</reference>). An appropriate retribution that Jerusalem, which consulted necromancers, should be made like them! <div eID="gen14731" type="x-p"/>
entries.63f85730c6743110d7674e5eb436a6bbc831cc27: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8834"/><div sID="gen14732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8834"/><hi type="bold">5. Moreover--</hi>rather, "Yet"; yet in this extremity help shall come, and the enemy be scattered.<div eID="gen14732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14733" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strangers--</hi>foreign enemies, invaders (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.2">Is 25:2</reference>).<div eID="gen14733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14734" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it shall be--</hi>namely, the destruction of the enemy.<div eID="gen14734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14735" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at an instant--</hi>in a moment (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.23">Is 30:23</reference>). <div eID="gen14735" type="x-p"/>
entries.55a4e5de873d1a41dc280317b7a26817f3be0907: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8835"/><div sID="gen14736" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8835"/><hi type="bold">6. Thou--</hi>the Assyrian army.<div eID="gen14736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14737" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thunder, &c.--</hi>not literally, in the case of the Assyrians (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Is 37:36</reference>); but figuratively for an awful judgment (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.30">Is 30:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.17">28:17</reference>). The ulterior fulfilment, in the case of the Jews' foes in the last days, may be more literal (see as to "earthquake," <reference osisRef="Zech.14.4">Zec 14:4</reference>). <div eID="gen14737" type="x-p"/>
entries.7859f342b67b1890a959a18d1c0750e16d942da6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8836"/><div sID="gen14738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8836"/><hi type="bold">7. munition--</hi>fortress. <div eID="gen14738" type="x-p"/>
entries.0909e1a9fb698a867f1a9ff5e595d29a8ecd56be: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8837"/><div sID="gen14739" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8837"/>8. Their disappointment in the very height of their confident expectation of taking Jerusalem shall be as great as that of the hungry man who in a dream fancies he eats, but awakes to hunger still (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.20">Psa 73:20</reference>); their dream shall be dissipated on the fatal morning (<reference osisRef="Isa.37.36">Is 37:36</reference>).<div eID="gen14739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14740" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">soul--</hi>simply his appetite: he is still thirsty. <div eID="gen14740" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa6c0a42ec7a953c13c4087fe4cd60a22dce3f8d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8838"/><div sID="gen14741" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8838"/><hi type="bold">9. Stay--</hi>rather, "Be astounded"; expressing the stupid and amazed incredulity with which the Jews received Isaiah's announcement.<div eID="gen14741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14742" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wonder--</hi>The second imperative, as often (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">Is 8:9</reference>), is a threat; the first is a simple declaration of a fact, "Be astounded, since you choose to be so, at the prophecy, soon you will be amazed at the sight of the actual event" [Maurer].<div eID="gen14742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14743" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cry ... out ... cry--</hi>rather, "Be ye blinded (since you choose to be so, though the light shines all round you), and soon ye shall be blinded" in good earnest to your sorrow [Maurer], (<reference osisRef="Isa.6.9">Is 6:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen14743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14744" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not with wine--</hi>but with spiritual paralysis (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.17">Is 51:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.21">21</reference>).<div eID="gen14744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14745" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye ... they--</hi>The change from speaking to, to speaking of them, intimates that the prophet turns away from them to a greater distance, because of their stupid unbelief. <div eID="gen14745" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae879b928a83cf2e67b0848399aebe1ea27ce2e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8839"/><div sID="gen14746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8839"/>10. Jehovah gives them up judicially to their own hardness of heart (compare <reference osisRef="Zech.14.13">Zec 14:13</reference>). Quoted by Paul, with variations from the Septuagint, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.8">Ro 11:8</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">Is 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.23">Psa 69:23</reference>.<div eID="gen14746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14747" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eyes; the prophets, &c.--</hi>rather, "hath closed your eyes, the prophets; and your heads (Margin; see also <reference osisRef="Isa.3.2">Is 3:2</reference>), the seers, He hath covered." The Orientals cover the head to sleep; thus "covered" is parallel to "closed your eyes" (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.19">Jud 4:19</reference>). Covering the face was also preparatory to execution (<reference osisRef="Esth.7.8">Es 7:8</reference>). This cannot apply to the time when Isaiah himself prophesied, but to subsequent times. <div eID="gen14747" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f1358577eef1b4a8f35f527749b1de416ea4088: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8840"/><div sID="gen14748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8840"/><hi type="bold">11. of all--</hi>rather, "the whole vision." "Vision" is the same here as "revelation," or "law"; in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.15">Is 28:15</reference>, the same Hebrew word is translated, "covenant" [Maurer].<div eID="gen14748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sealed--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.8.16">Is 8:16</reference>), God seals up the truth so that even the learned, because they lack believing docility, cannot discern it (Mt 13:10-17; 11:<reference osisRef="Matt.17.25">25</reference>). Prophecy remained comparatively a sealed volume (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.4">Da 12:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.9">9</reference>), until Jesus, who "alone is worthy," "opened the seals" (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.1-Rev.5.9">Re 5:1-5, 9</reference>; 6:1). <div eID="gen14749" type="x-p"/>
entries.9fa3544ad364e28b5f7b1aab0cf30ce29b51e09c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8841"/><div sID="gen14750" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8841"/>12. The unlearned succeed no better than the learned, not from want of human learning, as they fancy, but from not having the teaching of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.13">Is 54:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.34">Jr 31:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.45">Joh 6:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.7-1Cor.2.10">1Co 2:7-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.20">1Jo 2:20</reference>). <div eID="gen14750" type="x-p"/>
entries.474118d9c737215e47c252b50a9ef424853f89fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8842"/><div sID="gen14751" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8842"/><hi type="bold">13. precept of men--</hi>instead of the precepts of God, given by His prophets; also worship external, and by rule, not heartfelt as God requires (<reference osisRef="John.4.24">Joh 4:24</reference>). Compare Christ's quotation of this verse from the Septuagint. <div eID="gen14751" type="x-p"/>
entries.829d98cd5153901d7a3edeeacfa84a3528dd0fc2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8843"/><div sID="gen14752" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8843"/>14. (<reference osisRef="Hab.1.5">Ha 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.41">Ac 13:41</reference>). The "marvellous work" is one of unparalleled vengeance on the hypocrites: compare "strange work," <reference osisRef="Isa.28.21">Is 28:21</reference>. The judgment, too, will visit the wise in that respect in which they most pride themselves; their wisdom shall be hid, that is, shall no longer appear, so as to help the nation in its distress (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.19">1Co 1:19</reference>). <div eID="gen14752" type="x-p"/>
entries.d4f0a9d69f58504fbd7e9d7102ab4922ae12d68a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8844"/><div sID="gen14753" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8844"/><hi type="bold">15. seek deep to hide--</hi>rather, "That seek to hide deeply," &c. (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.30.1">Is 30:1</reference>, 2). The reference is to the secret plan which many of the Jewish nobles had of seeking Egyptian aid against Assyria, contrary to the advice of Isaiah. At the same time the hypocrite in general is described, who, under a plausible exterior, tries to hide his real character, not only from men, but even from God. <div eID="gen14753" type="x-p"/>
entries.f38b9ff00ad0d1a5070870ff70605db4400256e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8845"/><div sID="gen14754" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8845"/>16. Rather, "Ah! your perverseness! just as if the potter should be esteemed as the clay!" [Maurer]. Or, "Ye invert (turn upside down) the order of things, putting yourselves instead of God," and vice versa, just as if the potter should be esteemed as the clay [Horsley], (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">Is 45:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.64.8">64:8</reference>). <div eID="gen14754" type="x-p"/>
entries.c7804e6e3efa49cf19929c140501eef57a403171: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8846"/><div sID="gen14755" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8846"/><hi type="bold">17. turned--</hi>as contrasted with your "turnings of things upside down" (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.16">Is 29:16</reference>), there shall be other and better turnings or revolutions; the outpouring of the Spirit in the latter days (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.15">Is 32:15</reference>); first on the Jews; which shall be followed by their national restoration (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.29.2">Is 29:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>) then on the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Joel.2.28">Joe 2:28</reference>).<div eID="gen14755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14756" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fruitful field--</hi>literally, "a Carmel" (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.10.18">Is 10:18</reference>). The moral change in the Jewish nation shall be as great as if the wooded Lebanon were to become a fruitful field, and vice versa. Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.11.12">Mt 11:12</reference>, Greek: "the kingdom of heaven forces itself," as it were, on man's acceptance; instead of men having to seek Messiah, as they had John, in a desert, He presents Himself before them with loving invitations; thus men's hearts, once a moral desert, are reclaimed so as to bear fruits of righteousness: vice versa, the ungodly who seemed prosperous, both in the moral and literal sense, shall be exhibited in their real barrenness. <div eID="gen14756" type="x-p"/>
entries.10824cfdc1cd917ced8bfa4947e1c31991a8d7aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8847"/><div sID="gen14757" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8847"/><hi type="bold">18. deaf ... blind--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.11.5">Mt 11:5</reference>). The spiritually blind, &c., are chiefly meant; "the book," as Revelation is called pre-eminently, shall be no longer "sealed," as is described (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.11">Is 29:11</reference>), but the most unintelligent shall hear and see (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.5">Is 35:5</reference>). <div eID="gen14757" type="x-p"/>
entries.c61e81b5b9826308c4bed3ae47c6e5bb740f64c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8848"/><div sID="gen14758" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8848"/><hi type="bold">19. meek--</hi>rather, the afflicted godly: the idea is, virtuous suffering (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Is 61:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.25.9">Psa 25:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.11">37:11</reference>) [Barnes].<div eID="gen14758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">poor among men--</hi>that is, the poorest of men, namely, the pious poor.<div eID="gen14759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14760" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rejoice--</hi>when they see their oppressors punished (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.20">Is 29:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.21">21</reference>), and Jehovah exhibited as their protector and rewarder (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.22-Isa.29.24">Is 29:22-24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.17">Is 41:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.2.5">Jas 2:5</reference>). <div eID="gen14760" type="x-p"/>
entries.766e8bc63e0cb583900f440024ef37119d7998db: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8849"/><div sID="gen14761" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8849"/><hi type="bold">20. terrible--</hi>namely, the persecutors among the Jewish nobles.<div eID="gen14761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14762" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scorner--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.28.14">Is 28:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen14762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14763" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watch for--</hi>not only commit iniquity, but watch for opportunities of committing it, and make it their whole study (see <reference osisRef="Mic.2.1">Mi 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.59">Mt 26:59</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.27.1">27:1</reference>). <div eID="gen14763" type="x-p"/>
entries.b10923915857e097f5957bcdf449ae67f1c191ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8850"/><div sID="gen14764" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8850"/>21. Rather, "Who make a man guilty in his cause" [Gesenius], that is, unjustly condemn him. "A man" is in the Hebrew a poor man, upon whom such unjust condemnations might be practiced with more impunity than on the rich; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.29.19">Is 29:19</reference>, "the meek ... the poor."<div eID="gen14764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">him that reproveth--</hi>rather, "pleadeth"; one who has a suit at issue.<div eID="gen14765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14766" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gate--</hi>the place of concourse in a city, where courts of justice were held (<reference osisRef="Ruth.4.11">Ru 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.31.23">Pr 31:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.10">Am 5:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen14766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14767" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">just--</hi>one who has a just cause; or, Jesus Christ, "the Just One" [Horsley].<div eID="gen14767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14768" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for a thing of naught--</hi>rather, "through falsehood," "by a decision that is null in justice" [Barnes]. Compare as to Christ, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.21">Pr 28:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.26.15">Mt 26:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.3.13">Ac 3:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.3.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.8.33">8:33</reference>. <div eID="gen14768" type="x-p"/>
entries.66e1ec6150ffb3b60f4d47d28358d12c96a08be2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8851"/><div sID="gen14769" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8851"/>22. Join "saith ... concerning the house of Jacob."<div eID="gen14769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14770" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">redeemed--</hi>out of Ur, a land of idolaters (<reference osisRef="Josh.24.3">Jos 24:3</reference>).<div eID="gen14770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14771" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not now--</hi>After the moral revolution described (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.17">Is 29:17</reference>), the children of Jacob shall no longer give cause to their forefathers to blush for them.<div eID="gen14771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14772" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wax pale--</hi>with shame and disappointment at the wicked degeneracy of his posterity, and fear as to their punishment. <div eID="gen14772" type="x-p"/>
entries.da9472e706fec1d6b9667ac6ab3a4dfe0639d3d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8852"/><div sID="gen14773" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8852"/><hi type="bold">23. But--</hi>rather, "For."<div eID="gen14773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he--</hi>Jacob.<div eID="gen14774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14775" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">work of mine hands--</hi>spiritually, as well as physically (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.25">Is 19:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.60.21">60:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.10">Ep 2:10</reference>). By Jehovah's agency Israel shall be cleansed of its corruptions, and shall consist wholly of pious men (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.13">Is 54:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.14">14</reference>; 2:1; 60:21).<div eID="gen14775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14776" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">midst of him--</hi>that is, his land. Or else "His children" are the Gentiles adopted among the Israelites, his lineal descendants (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.26">Ro 9:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.6">Ep 3:6</reference>) [Horsley]. <div eID="gen14776" type="x-p"/>
entries.acdf20e5109ad458bffe7496b6df6d71ca3588c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8853"/><div sID="gen14777" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8853"/><hi type="bold">24. They ... that erred--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.28.7">Is 28:7</reference>).<div eID="gen14777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14778" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">learn doctrine--</hi>rather, "shall receive discipline" or "instruction." "Murmuring" was the characteristic of Israel's rebellion against God (<reference osisRef="Exod.16.8">Ex 16:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.25">Psa 106:25</reference>). This shall be so no more. Chastisements, and, in Horsley's view, the piety of the Gentiles provoking the Jews to holy jealousy (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.11">Ro 11:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.14">14</reference>), shall then produce the desired effect. <chapter eID="Isa.29"/>

entries.2d440ccb9d956917aa5d457fbbc0f59205198191: <div eID="gen27663" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27664" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27665" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27665" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27664" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27666" type="x-p"/> Distress of Ariel, or Jerusalem, on Sennacherib's invasion, with manifest allusion, however, to the still greater distress which it suffered from the Romans, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.1-Isa.29.4">Isa 29:1-4</reference>. Disappointment and fall of Sennacherib described in terms, like the event, the most awful and terrible, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.5-Isa.29.8">Isa 29:5-8</reference>. Stupidity and hypocrisy of the Jews, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.9-Isa.29.16">Isa 29:9-16</reference>. Rejection of the Jews, and calling of the Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.17">Isa 29:17</reference>. The chapter concludes by a recurrence to the favourite topics of the prophet, viz., the great extension of the Messiah's kingdom in the latter days, and the future restoration of Israel, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.18-Isa.29.24">Isa 29:18-24</reference>. <div eID="gen27666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27667" type="x-p"/> The subject of this and the four following chapters is the invasion of Sennacherib; the great distress of the Jews while it continued; their sudden and unexpected deliverance by God's immediate interposition in their favor; the subsequent prosperous state of the kingdom under Hezekiah; interspersed with severe reproofs, and threats of punishment, for their hypocrisy, stupidity, infidelity, their want of trust in God, and their vain reliance on the assistance of Egypt; and with promises of better times, both immediately to succeed, and to be expected in the future age. The whole making, not one continued discourse, but rather a collection of different discourses upon the same subject; which is treated with great elegance and variety. Though the matter is various, and the transitions sudden, yet the prophet seldom goes far from his subject. It is properly enough divided by the chapters in the common translation. - L. <div eID="gen27667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27668" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27669" type="x-p"/> Ariel - That Jerusalem is here called by this name is very certain: but the reason of this name, and the meaning of it as applied to Jerusalem, is very obscure and doubtful. Some, with the Chaldee, suppose it to be taken from the hearth of the great altar of burnt-offerings which Ezekiel plainly calls by the same name, and that Jerusalem is here considered as the seat of the fire of God, אור אל ur el which should issue from thence to consume his enemies: compare <reference osisRef="Isa.31.9">Isa 31:9</reference>. Some, according to the common derivation of the word, ארי אל ari el, the lion of God, or the strong lion, suppose it to signify the strength of the place, by which it was enabled to resist and overcome all its enemies. Τινες δε φασι την πολιν οὑτως ειρησθαι· επει, δια Θεου, λεοντος δικην εσπαραττε τους ανταιροντας. Procop. in loc. There are other explanations of this name given: but none that seems to be perfectly satisfactory. - Lowth. <div eID="gen27669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27670" type="x-p"/> From <reference osisRef="Eze.43.15">Eze 43:15</reference>, we learn that Ari-el was the name of the altar of burnt-offerings, put here for the city itself in which that altar was. In the second verse it is said, I will distress Ari-el, and it shall be unto me as Ari-el. The first Ari-el here seems to mean Jerusalem, which should be distressed by the Assyrians: the second Ari-el seems to mean the altar of burntofferings. But why is it said, "Ari-el shall be unto me as Ari-el?" As the altar of burntofferings was surrounded daily by the victims which were offered: so the walls of Jerusalem shall be surrounded by the dead bodies of those who had rebelled against the Lord, and who should be victims to his justice. The translation of Bishop Lowth appears to embrace both meanings: "I will bring distress upon Ari-el; and it shall be to me as the hearth of the great altar." <div eID="gen27670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27671" type="x-p"/> Add ye year to year - Ironically. Go on year after year, keep your solemn feasts; yet know, that God will punish you for your hypocritical worship, consisting of mere form destitute of true piety. Probably delivered at the time of some great feast, when they were thus employed.
entries.51a4077b76d91c57b60af48d723d95740839ca85: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen27671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27672" type="x-p"/> There shall be heaviness and sorrow "There shall be continual mourning and sorrow" - Instead of your present joy and festivity. <div eID="gen27672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27673" type="x-p"/> And it shall be unto me as Ariel "And it shall be unto me as the hearth of the great altar" - That is, it shall be the seat of the fire of God; which shall issue from thence to consume his enemies. See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.29.1">Isa 29:1</reference> (note). Or, perhaps, all on flame; as it was when taken by the Chaldeans; or covered with carcasses and blood, as when taken by the Romans: an intimation of which more distant events, though not immediate subjects of the prophecy, may perhaps be given in this obscure passage.
entries.5ce7b28758e44456fa1aba66113dbb3469434e1d: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen27673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27674" type="x-p"/> And I will camp against thee round about "And I will encamp against thee like David" - For כדור caddur, some kind of military engine, כדוד kedavid, like David, is the reading of the Septuagint, two MSS. of Kennicott's, if not two more: but though Bishop Lowth adopts this reading, I think it harsh and unnecessary. <div eID="gen27674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27675" type="x-p"/> Forts "Towers" - For מצרת metsuroth, read מצדות metsudoth: so the Septuagint and five MSS. of Dr. Kennicott's, one of them ancient, and four of De Rossi's.
entries.bf536565292cf0a46bc55e7766a45b230af51948: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27676" type="x-p"/> And thy speech shall be low out of the dust "And from out of the dust thou shalt utter a feeble speech" - That the souls of the dead uttered a feeble stridulous sound, very different from the natural human voice, was a popular notion among the heathens as well as among the Jews. This appears from several passages of their poets; Homer, Virgil, Horace. The pretenders to the art of necromancy, who were chiefly women, had an art of speaking with a feigned voice, so as to deceive those who applied to them, by making them believe that it was the voice of the ghost. They had a way of uttering sounds, as if they were formed, not by the organs of speech, but deep in the chest, or in the belly; and were thence called εγγαστριμυθοι, ventriloqui: they could make the voice seem to come from beneath the ground, from a distant part, in another direction, and not from themselves; the better to impose upon those who consulted them. Εξεπιτηδες το γενος τουτο τον αμυδρον ηχον επιτηδευονται, ἱνα δια την ασαφειαν της φωνης τον του ψευδους αποδιδρασκωσιν ελεγχον. Psellus De Daemonibus, apud Bochart, 1 p. 731. "These people studiously acquire, and affect on purpose, this sort of obscure sound; that by the uncertainty of the voice they may the better escape being detected in the cheat. "From these arts of the necromancers the popular notion seems to have arisen, that the ghost's voice was a weak, stridulous, almost inarticulate sort of sound, very different from the speech of the living.
