entries.cf24d85d8adc9572d8aec6673b30c0e3c1682464: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27677" type="x-p"/> The multitude of thy strangers "The multitude of the proud" - For זריך zarayich, thy strangers, read זדים zedim, the proud, according to the Septuagint; parallel to and synonymous with עריצים aritsim, the terrible, in the next line: the ר resh was at first ד daleth in a MS. See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.25.2">Isa 25:2</reference>. <div eID="gen27677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27678" type="x-p"/> The fifth, sixth, and seventh verses contain an admirable description of the destruction of Sennacherib's army, with a beautiful variety of the most expressive and sublime images: perhaps more adapted to show the greatness, the suddenness, and horror of the event, than the means and manner by which it was effected. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.30.30-Isa.30.33">Isa 30:30-33</reference>.
entries.c5767c7700bc66a20b5a36ddbf5ba907c13e86d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen27678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27679" type="x-p"/> As a dream - This is the beginning of the comparison, which is pursued and applied in the next verse. Sennacherib and his mighty army are not compared to a dream because of their sudden disappearance; but the disappointment of their eager hopes is compared to what happens to a hungry and thirsty man, when he awakes from a dream in which fancy had presented to him meat and drink in abundance, and finds it nothing but a vain illusion. The comparison is elegant and beautiful in the highest degree, well wrought up, and perfectly suited to the end proposed. The image is extremely natural, but not obvious: it appeals to our inward feelings, not to our outward senses; and is applied to an event in its concomitant circumstances exactly similar, but in its nature totally different. See De S. Poes. Hebr. Praelect. 12. For beauty and ingenuity it may fairly come in competition with one of the most elegant of Virgil, greatly improved from Homer, Iliad 22:199, where he has applied to a different purpose, but not so happily, the same image of the ineffectual working of imagination in a dream: - <div eID="gen27679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27680" type="x-p"/> Ac veluti in somnis, oculos ubi languida pressit <div eID="gen27680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27681" type="x-p"/> Nocte quies, necquicquam avidos extendere cursus <div eID="gen27681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27682" type="x-p"/> Velle videmur, et in mediis conatibus aegri <div eID="gen27682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27683" type="x-p"/> Succidimus; non lingua valet, non corpore notae <div eID="gen27683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27684" type="x-p"/> Sufficiunt vires, nec vox, nec verba sequuntur. <div eID="gen27684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27685" type="x-p"/> Aen., 12:908. "And as, when slumber seals the closing sight, <div eID="gen27685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27686" type="x-p"/> The sick wild fancy labors in the night; <div eID="gen27686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27687" type="x-p"/> Some dreadful visionary foe we shun <div eID="gen27687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27688" type="x-p"/> With airy strides, but strive in vain to run; <div eID="gen27688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27689" type="x-p"/> In vain our baffled limbs their powers essay; <div eID="gen27689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27690" type="x-p"/> We faint, we struggle, sink, and fall away; <div eID="gen27690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27691" type="x-p"/> Drain'd of our strength, we neither fight nor fly, <div eID="gen27691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27692" type="x-p"/> And on the tongue the struggling accents die." <div eID="gen27692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27693" type="x-p"/> Pitt. <div eID="gen27693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27694" type="x-p"/> Lucretius expresses the very same image with Isaiah: - <div eID="gen27694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27695" type="x-p"/> Ut bibere in somnis sitiens quum quaerit, et humor <div eID="gen27695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27696" type="x-p"/> Non datur, ardorem in membris qui stinguere possit; <div eID="gen27696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27697" type="x-p"/> Sed laticum simulacra petit, frustraque laborat, <div eID="gen27697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27698" type="x-p"/> In medioque sitit torrenti flumine potans. <div eID="gen27698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27699" type="x-p"/> As a thirsty man desires to drink in his sleep, <div eID="gen27699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27700" type="x-p"/> And has no fluid to allay the heat within, <div eID="gen27700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27701" type="x-p"/> But vainly labors to catch the image of rivers, <div eID="gen27701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27702" type="x-p"/> And is parched up while fancying that he is drinking at a full stream. <div eID="gen27702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27703" type="x-p"/> Bishop Stock's translation of the prophet's text is both elegant and just: - "As when a hungry man dreameth; and, lo! he is eating: <div eID="gen27703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27704" type="x-p"/> And he awaketh; and his appetite is unsatisfied. <div eID="gen27704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27705" type="x-p"/> And as a thirsty man dreameth; and, lo! he is drinking: <div eID="gen27705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27706" type="x-p"/> And he awaketh; and, lo! he is faint, <div eID="gen27706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27707" type="x-p"/> And his appetite craveth." <div eID="gen27707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27708" type="x-p"/> Lucretius almost copies the original. <div eID="gen27708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27709" type="x-p"/> All that fight against her and her munition "And all their armies and their towers" - For צביה ומצדתה tsobeyha umetsodathah, I read, with the Chaldee, צבאם ומצדתם tsebaam umetsodatham.
entries.2a7fa4b71f59c3c9ae13224dfe61a95b251628c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen27709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27710" type="x-p"/> Stay yourselves, and wonder - התמהמהו hithmahmehu, go on what-what-whatting, in a state of mental indetermination, till the overflowing scourge take you away. See the note on <reference osisRef="Psa.119.60">Psa 119:60</reference> (note). <div eID="gen27710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27711" type="x-p"/> They are drunken, but not with wine - See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.51.21">Isa 51:21</reference>.
entries.5de09bad8db94eaa3a4492f652efdaeb6d925ffd: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen27711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27712" type="x-p"/> I cannot; for it is sealed "I cannot read it; for it is sealed up" - An ancient MS. and the Septuagint have preserved a word here, lost out of the text; לקרות likroth, (for לקראות), αναγνωναι, read it.
entries.8f5aba146184860c334c9de142b0039547c71536: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen27712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27713" type="x-p"/> The Lord "Jehovah" - For אדני Adonai, sixty-three MSS. of Kennicott's, and many of De Rossi's, and four editions, read יהוה Yehovah, and five MSS. add יהוה. <div eID="gen27713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27714" type="x-p"/> Kimchi makes some just observations on this verse. The vision, meaning the Divine revelation of all the prophets, is a book or letter that is sealed - is not easily understood. This is delivered to one that is learned - instructed in the law. Read this; and he saith, I cannot, for it is sealed; a full proof that he does not wish to know the contents else he would apply to the prophet to get it explained. See Kimchi on the place. <div eID="gen27714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27715" type="x-p"/> And their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men "And vain is their fear of me teaching the commandments of men" - I read for ותהי vattehi, ותהו vethohu, with the Septuagint, <reference osisRef="Mat.15.9">Mat 15:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mar.8.7">Mar 8:7</reference>; and for מלמדה melummedah, מלמדים melummedim, with the Chaldee.
entries.ca9f9de98c421010fa489ccab366cb6dc6fca30a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen27715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27716" type="x-p"/> And Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field "Ere Lebanon become like Carmel" - A mashal, or proverbial saying, expressing any great revolution of things; and, when respecting two subjects, an entire reciprocal change: explained here by some interpreters, I think with great probability, as having its principal view beyond the revolutions then near at hand, to the rejection of the Jews, and the calling of the Gentiles. The first were the vineyard of God, כרם אל kerem El, (if the prophet, who loves an allusion to words of like sounds, may be supposed to have intended one here), cultivated and watered by him in vain, to be given up, and to become a wilderness: compare <reference osisRef="Isa.5.1-Isa.5.7">Isa 5:1-7</reference>. The last had been hitherto barren; but were, by the grace of God, to be rendered fruitful. See <reference osisRef="Mat.21.43">Mat 21:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.30">Rom 11:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.31">Rom 11:31</reference>. Carmel stands here opposed to Lebanon, and therefore is to be taken as a proper name.
entries.9fc760e0a043f490e29101469af83e5a8706ea34: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen27716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27717" type="x-p"/> Him that reproveth in the gate "Him that pleaded in the gate" - "They are heard by the treasurer, master of the horse, and other principal officers of the regency of Algiers, who sit constantly in the gate of the palace for that purpose:" that is, the distribution of justice. - Shaw's Travels, p. 315, fol. He adds in the note, "That we read of the elders in the gate. <reference osisRef="Deu.21.15">Deu 21:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deu.25.7">Deu 25:7</reference>; and, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.21">Isa 29:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amo.5.10">Amo 5:10</reference>, of him that reproveth and rebuketh in the gate. The Ottoman court likewise seems to have been called the Porte, from the distribution of justice and the dispatch of public business that is carried on in the gates of it."
entries.c48f55fb6a3e673d82f6dce521293acebf66ac7d: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen27717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27718" type="x-p"/> Who redeemed Abraham - As God redeemed Abraham from among idolaters and workers of iniquity, so will he redeem those who hear the words of the Book, and are humbled before him, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.18">Isa 29:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.19">Isa 29:19</reference>. <div eID="gen27718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27719" type="x-p"/> Concerning the house of Jacob "The God of the house of Jacob" - I read אל El as a noun, not a preposition: the parallel line favors this sense; and there is no address to the house of Jacob to justify the other. <div eID="gen27719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27720" type="x-p"/> Neither shall his face now wax pale "His face shall no more be covered with confusion" - "יחורו yechoro, Chald. ut ὁ μεταβαλει, Theod. εντραπησεται, Syr. נחפרו necaphro, videtur legendum יחפרו yechepheru: hic enim solum legitur verbum, חור chavar, nec in linguis affinibus habet pudoris significationem." - Secker. "Here alone is the verb חור charar read; nor has it in the cognate languages the signification of shame."
entries.205c570a5915d29fc276bbea40f311a5c6602b37: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen27720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27721" type="x-p"/> But when he seeth his children, the work of mine hands "For when his children shall see the work of my hands" - For בראותו birotho I read בראות biroth, with the Septuagint and Syriac.  <chapter eID="Isa.29"/> <div eID="gen27721" type="x-p"/>

entries.b7340492fc8b5bb8fa9ecbab95feec1f165ca1f0: <reference osisRef="Isa.29.1-Isa.29.4">Isa 29:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen13177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13178" type="x-p"/> The prophecy here passes from the fall of Samaria, the crown of flowers (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.1-Isa.28.4">Isa 28:1-4</reference>), to its formal parallel. Jerusalem takes its place by the side of Samaria, the crown of flowers, and under the emblem of a hearth of God. <hi type="italic">'Arı̄'ēl</hi> might, indeed, mean a lion of God. It occurs in this sense as the name of certain Moabitish heroes (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.20">2Sa 23:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.22">1Ch 11:22</reference>), and Isaiah himself used the shorter form אראל for the heroes of Judah (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.7">Isa 33:7</reference>). But as אריאל (God’s heart, interchanged with הראל htiw degna, God’s height) is the name given in <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.15-Ezek.43.16">Eze 43:15-16</reference>, to the altar of burnt-offering in the new temple, and as Isaiah could not say anything more characteristic of Jerusalem, than that Jehovah had a fire and hearth there (<reference osisRef="Isa.31.9">Isa 31:9</reference>); and, moreover, as Jerusalem the city and community within the city would have been compared to a lioness rather than a lion, we take אריאל in the sense of <hi type="italic">ara Dei</hi> (from ארה, to burn). The prophet commences in his own peculiar way with a grand summary introduction, which passes in a few gigantic strides over the whole course from threatening to promise. <reference osisRef="Isa.29.1">Isa 29:1</reference> <hi type="italic">“Woe to Ariel, to Ariel, the castle where David pitched his tent! Add year to year, let the feasts revolve: then I distress Ariel, and there is groaning and moaning; and so she proves herself to me as Ariel.”</hi> By the fact that David fixed his headquarters in Jerusalem, and then brought the sacred ark thither, Jerusalem became a hearth of God. Within a single year, after only one more round of feasts (to be interpreted according to <reference osisRef="Isa.32.10">Isa 32:10</reference>, and probably spoken at the passover), Jehovah would make Jerusalem a besieged city, full of sighs (<hi type="italic">vahătsı̄qōthı̄</hi>, <hi type="italic">perf. cons.</hi>, with the tone upon the ultimate); but “she becomes to me like an <hi type="italic">Arı̄el</hi>,” i.e., being qualified through me, she will prove herself a hearth of God, by consuming the foes like a furnace, or by their meeting with their destruction at Jerusalem, like wood piled up on the altar and then consumed in flame. The prophecy has thus passed over the whole ground in a few majestic words. It now starts from the very beginning again, and first of all expands the <hi type="italic">hoi</hi>. <reference osisRef="Isa.29.3">Isa 29:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.4">Isa 29:4</reference> <hi type="italic">“And I encamp in a circle round about thee, and surround thee with watch-posts, and erect tortoises against thee. And when brought down thou wilt speak from out of the ground, and thy speaking will sound low out of the dust; and thy voice cometh up like that of a demon from the ground, and thy speaking will whisper out of the dust.”</hi> It would have to go so far with Ariel first of all, that it would be besieged by a hostile force, and would lie upon the ground in the greatest extremity, and then would whisper with a ghostlike softness, like a dying man, or like a spirit without flesh and bones. <hi type="italic">Kaddūr</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">sphaera</hi>, <hi type="italic">orbis</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.22.18">Isa 22:18</reference> and in the Talmud (from <hi type="italic">kâdar</hi> = <hi type="italic">kâthar</hi>; cf., <hi type="italic">kudur</hi> in the name <hi type="italic">Nabu</hi>-<hi type="italic">kudur</hi>-<hi type="italic">ussur</hi>, Nebo protect the crown, κίδαριν), and is used here poetically for סביב. Jerome renders it <hi type="italic">quasi sphaeram</hi> (from <hi type="italic">dūr</hi>, <hi type="italic">orbis</hi>). מצּב (from נצב, יצב) might signify “firmly planted” (Luzzatto, <hi type="italic">immobilmente</hi>; compare <hi type="italic">shūth</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.7">Isa 2:7</reference>); but according to the parallel it signifies a military post, like מצּב, נציב. <hi type="italic">Metsurōth</hi> (from <hi type="italic">mâtsōr</hi>, <reference osisRef="Deut.20.20">Deu 20:20</reference>) are instruments of siege, the nature of which can only be determined conjecturally. On <hi type="italic">'ōbh</hi>, see <reference osisRef="Isa.8.19">Isa 8:19</reference>;<note placement="foot">The <hi type="italic">'akkuubh</hi> mentioned there is equivalent to <hi type="italic">anbûb</hi>, Arab. a knot on a reed stalk, then that part of such a reed which comes between two knots, then the reed stalk itself; root נב, to rise up, swell, or become convex without and concave within (Fl.). It is possible that it would be better to trace <hi type="italic">'ōbh</hi> back to this radical and primary meaning of what is hollow (and therefore has a dull sound), whether used in the sense of a leather-bag, or applied to a spirit of incantation, and the possessor of such a spirit.</note> there is no necessity to take it as standing for <hi type="italic">ba‛al 'ōbh</hi>.
entries.adaa4d923cbebda42841cd1ebd56278c41bbb461: <reference osisRef="Isa.29.5-Isa.29.8">Isa 29:5-8</reference> <div eID="gen13178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13179" type="x-p"/> Thus far does the unfolding of the <hi type="italic">hoi</hi> reach. Now follows an unfolding of the words of promise, which stand at the end of <reference osisRef="Isa.29.1">Isa 29:1</reference> : <hi type="italic">“And it proves itself to me as Ariel.”</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.29.5-Isa.29.8">Isa 29:5-8</reference> : <hi type="italic">“And the multitude of thy foes will become like finely powdered dust, and the multitude of the tyrants like chaff flying away; and it will take place suddenly, very suddenly. From Jehovah of hosts there comes a visitation with crash of thunder and earthquake and great noise, whirlwind and tempest, and the blazing up of devouring fire. And the multitude of all the nations that gather together against Ariel, and all those who storm and distress Ariel and her stronghold, will be like a vision of the night in a dream. And it is just as a hungry man dreams, and behold he eats; and when he wakes up his soul is empty: and just as a thirsty man dreams, and behold he drinks; and when he wakes up, behold, he is faint, and his soul is parched with thirst: so will it be to the multitude of the nations which gather together against the mountain of Zion.”</hi> The hostile army, described four times as <hi type="italic">hâmōn</hi>, a groaning multitude, is utterly annihilated through the terrible co-operation of the forces of nature which are let loose upon them (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.30">Isa 30:30</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.17.13">Isa 17:13</reference>). “<hi type="italic">There comes a visitation:</hi>” <hi type="italic">tippâqēd</hi> might refer to Jerusalem in the sense of “it will be visited” in mercy, viz., by Jehovah acting thus upon its enemies. But it is better to take it in a neuter sense: “punishment is inflicted.” The simile of the dream is applied in two different ways: (1.) They will dissolve into nothing, as if they had only the same apparent existence as a vision in a dream. (2.) Their plan for taking Jerusalem will be put to shame, and as utterly brought to nought as the eating or drinking of a dreamer, which turns out to be a delusion as soon as he awakes. Just as the prophet emphatically combines two substantives from the same verbal root in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.1">Isa 29:1</reference>, and two adverbs from the same verb in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.5">Isa 29:5</reference>; so does he place צבא and צבה together in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.7">Isa 29:7</reference>, the former with על relating to the crowding of an army for the purpose of a siege, the latter with an objective suffix (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.53.6">Psa 53:6</reference>) to the attack made by a crowded army. The <hi type="italic">metsōdâh</hi> of Ariel (i.e., the watch-tower, <hi type="italic">specula</hi>, from <hi type="italic">tsūd</hi>, to spy)<note placement="foot">In Arabic, also, <hi type="italic">masâd</hi> signifies a lofty hill or mountain-top, from a secondary form of <hi type="italic">tsud</hi>; and <hi type="italic">massara</hi>, to lay the foundations of a fortified city (<hi type="italic">‛ı̄r mâtsōr</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.22">Psa 31:22</reference>), from <hi type="italic">tsūr</hi>.)</note> is the mountain of Zion mentioned afterwards in Isa 29:8. כּאשׁר, as if; comp. Zec 10:6; Job 10:19. אוכל והנּה without הוּא; the personal pronoun is frequently omitted, not only in the leading participial clause, as in this instance (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.26.3">Isa 26:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.19">Isa 40:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.29">Psa 22:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.25.2">Job 25:2</reference>; and Köhler on Zec 9:12), but also with a minor participial clause, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.7.10">Psa 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.20">Psa 55:20</reference>, and Hab 2:10. The hungering and thirsting of the waking man are attributed to his <hi type="italic">nephesh</hi> (soul: cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.32.6">Isa 32:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.14">Isa 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.6.30">Pro 6:30</reference>), just because the soul is the cause of the physical life, and without it the action of the senses would be followed by no sensation or experience whatever. The hungry stomach is simply the object of feeling, and everything sensitive in the bodily organism is merely the medium of sensation or feeling; that which really <hi type="italic">feels</hi> is the soul. The soul no sooner passes out of the dreaming state into a waking condition, than it feels that its desires are as unsatisfied as ever. Just like such a dream will the army of the enemy, and that victory of which it is so certain before the battle is fought, fade away into nothing.
entries.b48d66b1d249247f809f34a01af7d8da6b779222: <reference osisRef="Isa.29.9-Isa.29.12">Isa 29:9-12</reference> <div eID="gen13179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13180" type="x-p"/> This enigma of the future the prophet holds out before the eyes of his contemporaries. The prophet received it by revelation of Jehovah; and without the illumination of Jehovah it could not possibly be understood. The deep degradation of Ariel, the wonderful deliverance, the sudden elevation from the abyss to this lofty height - all this was a matter of faith. But this faith was just what the nation wanted, and therefore the understanding depending upon it was wanting also. The <hi type="italic">shemu‛âh</hi> was there, but the <hi type="italic">bı̄nâh</hi> was absent; and all שׁמועה הבין was wrecked on the obtuseness of the mass. The prophet, therefore, who had received the unhappy calling to harden his people, could not help exclaiming (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.29.9">Isa 29:9</reference></hi>), “<hi type="italic">Stop, and stare; blind yourselves, and grow blind!</hi>” התמהמהּ, to show one’s self delaying (from מההּ, according to Luzzatto the reflective of תּמהמהּ, an emphatic form which is never met with), is connected with the synonymous verb תּמהּ, to be stiff with astonishment; but to שׁעע, to be plastered up, i.e., incapable of seeing (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">Isa 6:10</reference>), there is attached the <hi type="italic">hithpalpel</hi> of the same verb, signifying “to place one’s self in such circumstances,” <hi type="italic">se oblinere</hi> (differently, however, in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.16">Psa 119:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.47">Psa 119:47</reference>, compare <reference osisRef="Isa.11.8">Isa 11:8</reference>, <hi type="italic">se permulcere</hi>). They could not understand the word of God, but they were confused, and their eyes were, so to speak, festered up: therefore this self-induced condition would become to them a God-appointed punishment. The imperatives are judicial words of command. <div eID="gen13180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13181" type="x-p"/> This growth of the self-hardening into a judicial sentence of obduracy, is proclaimed still more fully by the prophet. <hi type="italic">“They are drunken, and not with wine; they reel, and not with meth. For Jehovah hath poured upon you a spirit of deep sleep, and bound up your eyes; the prophets and your heads, the seers, He has veiled. And the revelation of all this will be to you like words of a sealed writing, which they give to him who understands writing, saying, Pray, read this; but he says, I cannot, it is sealed. And they give the writing to one who does not understand writing, saying, Pray, read this; but he says, I do not understand writing.”</hi> They were drunken and stupid; not, however, merely because they gave themselves up to sensual intoxication (יין, dependent upon שׁכרוּ, <hi type="italic">ebrii vino</hi>), but because Jehovah had given them up to spiritual confusion and self-destruction. All the punishments of God are inflicted through the medium of His no less world-destroying than world-sustaining Spirit, which, although not willing what is evil, does make the evil called into existence by the creature the means of punishing evil. <hi type="italic">Tardēmâh</hi> is used here to signify the powerless, passive state of utter spiritual insensibility. This judgment had fallen upon the nation in all its members, even upon the eyes and heads of the nation, i.e., the prophets. Even they whose duty is was to see to the good of the nation, and lead it, were blind leaders of the blind; their eyes were fast shut (עצּם, the intensive form of the <hi type="italic">kal</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.15">Isa 33:15</reference>; Aram. עצּם; <hi type="italic">Talmud</hi> also עמּץ: to shut the eyes, or press them close), and over their heads a cover was drawn, as over sleepers in the night. Since the time of Koppe and Eichhorn it has become a usual thing to regard את־הנּביאים and החזים as a gloss, and indeed as a false one (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.9.13-Isa.9.14">Isa 9:13-14</reference>); but the reason assigned - namely, that Isaiah’s polemics are directed not against the prophets, but against the stupid staring people - is utterly groundless (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.28.7">Isa 28:7</reference>, and the polemics of his contemporary Micah, e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.3.5-Isa.3.8">Isa 3:5-8</reference>). Moreover, the author of a gloss would have been more likely to interpret ראשׁיכם by השּׂרים or הכּהנים (compare <reference osisRef="Job.9.24">Job 9:24</reference>). And <reference osisRef="Isa.29.11">Isa 29:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.12">Isa 29:12</reference> are also opposed to this assumption of a gloss. For by those who understood what was written (<hi type="italic">sēpher</hi>), it is evident that the prophets and rulers of the nation are intended; and by those who did not understand it, the great mass of the people. To both of them, “the vision of all,” i.e., of all and everything that God had shown to His true prophets, was by the judgment of God completely sealed. Some of them might have an outward knowledge; but the inward understanding of the revelation was sealed to them. Some had not even this, but stared at the word of the prophet, just as a man who cannot read stares at what is written. The <hi type="italic">chethib</hi> has הסּפר; the <hi type="italic">keri</hi> ספר, though without any ground, since the article is merely generic. Instead of נא־זה קרא, we should write זה קרא־נא in both cases, as certain codices and old editions do.
entries.ae48fe2d48add73214844c268d36bab1095ec41e: <reference osisRef="Isa.29.13-Isa.29.14">Isa 29:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen13181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13182" type="x-p"/> This stupefaction was the self-inflicted punishment of the dead works with which the people mocked God and deceived themselves. <hi type="italic">“The Lord hath spoken: Because this people approaches me with its mouth, and honours me with its lips, and keeps its heart far from me, and its reverence of me has become a commandment learned from men: therefore, behold, I will proceed wondrously with this people, wondrously and marvellously strange; and the wisdom of its wise men is lost, and the understanding of its intelligent men becomes invisible.”</hi> Ever since the time of Asaph (Ps 50, cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.78.36-Ps.78.37">Psa 78:36-37</reference>), the lamentation and condemnation of hypocritical ceremonial worship, without living faith or any striving after holiness, had been a leading theme of prophecy. Even in Isaiah’s introductory address (chapter 1) this complain was uttered quite in the tone of that of Asaph. In the time of Hezekiah it was peculiarly called for, just as it was afterwards in that of Josiah (as the book of Jeremiah shows). The people had been obliged to consent to the abolition of the public worship of idols, but their worship of Jehovah was hypocrisy. Sometimes it was conscious hypocrisy, arising from the fear of man and favour of man; sometimes unconscious, inasmuch as without any inward conversion, but simply with work-righteousness, the people contented themselves with, and even prided themselves upon, an outward fulfilment of the law (Mic 6:6-8; Mic 3:11). Instead of נגּשׁ (lxx, Vulg., Syr., <reference osisRef="Matt.15.8">Mat 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.7.6">Mar 7:6</reference>), we also meet with the reading נגּשׂ, “because this people harasses itself as with tributary service;” but the antithesis to <hi type="italic">richaq</hi> (lxx πόῤῥω ἀπέχει ) favours the former reading <hi type="italic">niggash</hi>, <hi type="italic">accedit</hi>; and <hi type="italic">bephı̄v</hi> (with its moth) must be connected with this, though in opposition to the accents. This self-alienation and self-blinding, Jehovah would punish with a wondrously paradoxical judgment, namely, the judgment of a hardening, which would so completely empty and confuse, that even the appearance of wisdom and unity, which the leaders of Israel still had, would completely disappear. יוסיף (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.38.5">Isa 38:5</reference>) is not the third person <hi type="italic">fut. hiphil</hi> here (so that it could be rendered, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Isa 28:16</reference>, “Behold, I am he who;” or more strictly still, “Behold me, who;” which, however, would give a prominence to the subject that would be out of place here), but the <hi type="italic">part.</hi> <hi type="italic">kal</hi> for יוסף. That the language really allowed of such a lengthening of the primary form <hi type="italic">qatĭl</hi> into <hi type="italic">qatı̄l</hi>, and especially in the case of יוסיף, is evident from <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.18">Ecc 1:18</reference> (see at <reference osisRef="Ps.16.5">Psa 16:5</reference>). In ופלא הפלא, פלא (cf., <reference osisRef="Lam.1.9">Lam 1:9</reference>) alternates with the gerundive (see at <reference osisRef="Isa.22.17">Isa 22:17</reference>): the fifth example in this one address of the emphatic juxtaposition of words having a similar sound and the same derivation (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.29.1">Isa 29:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.5">Isa 29:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.7">Isa 29:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.29.9">Isa 29:9</reference>).
entries.73a40ed3ee19b4aeb22ddbccace0eec20014a5e5: <reference osisRef="Isa.29.15-Isa.29.16">Isa 29:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen13182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13183" type="x-p"/> Their hypocrisy, which was about to be so wonderfully punished according to the universal law (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.26-Ps.18.27">Psa 18:26-27</reference>), manifested itself in their self-willed and secret behaviour, which would not inquire for Jehovah, nor suffer itself to be chastened by His word. <hi type="italic">“Woe unto them that hide plans deep from Jehovah, and their doing occurs in a dark place, and they say, Who saw us then, and who knew about us? Oh for your perversity! It is to be regarded as potters’ clay; that a work could say to its maker, He has not made me; and an image to its sculptor, He does not understand it!”</hi> Just as Ahaz had carefully kept his appeal to Asshur for help secret from the prophet; so did they try, as far as possible, to hide from the prophet the plan for an alliance with Egypt. לסתּיר is a syncopated <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> for להסתּיר, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.12">Isa 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.8">Isa 3:8</reference>; Isa 23:11. העמיק adds the adverbial notion, according to our mode of expression (comp. <reference osisRef="Joel.2.20">Joe 2:20</reference>, and the opposite thought in <reference osisRef="Joel.2.26">Joe 2:26</reference>; Ges. §142). To hide from Jehovah is equivalent to hiding from the prophet of Jehovah, that they might not have to listen to reproof from the word of Jehovah. We may see from <reference osisRef="Isa.8.12">Isa 8:12</reference> how suspiciously they watched the prophet in such circumstances as these. But Jehovah saw them in their secrecy, and the prophet saw through the whole in the light of Jehovah. הפכּכם is an exclamation, like תּפלצתּך in Jer 49:16. They are perverse, or (<hi type="italic">'im</hi>) “is it not so?” They think they can dispense with Jehovah, and yet they are His creatures; they attribute cleverness to themselves, and practically disown Jehovah, as if the pot should say to the potter who has turned it, He does not understand it.
entries.5f853518022046bac71df70fff25d59cbfd60e30: <reference osisRef="Isa.29.17-Isa.29.21">Isa 29:17-21</reference> <div eID="gen13183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13184" type="x-p"/> But the prophet’s God, whose omniscience, creative glory, and perfect wisdom they so basely mistook and ignored, would very shortly turn the present state of the world upside down, and make Himself a congregation out of the poor and wretched, whilst He would entirely destroy this proud ungodly nation. <hi type="italic">“Is it not yet a very little, and Lebanon is turned into a fruitful field, and the fruitful field esteemed as a forest? And in that day the deaf hear scripture words, and the eyes of the blind will see out of obscurity and out of darkness. And the joy of the humble increases in Jehovah, and the poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel. For tyrants are gone, and it is over with scoffers; and all who think evil are rooted out, who condemn a man for a word, and lay snares for him that is free-spoken in the gate, and overthrow the righteous through shameful lies.”</hi> The circumstances themselves, as well as the sentence passed, will experience a change, in complete contrast with the present state of things. This is what is affirmed in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.17">Isa 29:17</reference>; probably a proverb transposed into a more literary style. What is now forest becomes ennobled into garden ground; and what is garden ground becomes in general estimation a forest (לכרמל, ליער, although we should rather expect ל, just as in <reference osisRef="Isa.32.15">Isa 32:15</reference>). These emblems are explained in Isa 29:18. The people that are now blind and deaf, so far as the word of Jehovah is concerned, are changed into a people with open ears and seeing eyes. Scripture words, like those which the prophet now holds before the people so unsuccessfully, are heard by those who have been deaf. The unfettered sight of those who have been blind pierces through the hitherto surrounding darkness. The heirs of the new future thus transformed are the <hi type="italic">anâvı̄m</hi> (“meek”) and the <hi type="italic">'ebhyōnı̄m</hi> (“poor”). אדם (the antithesis of אנשׁהים, e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.29.13">Isa 29:13</reference>) heightens the representation of lowliness; the combination is a superlative one, as in הצאן צעירי, <reference osisRef="Jer.49.20">Jer 49:20</reference>, and הצאן עניי in Zec 11:7 (cf., חיות פריץ in <reference osisRef="Isa.35.9">Isa 35:9</reference>): needy men who present a glaring contrast to, and stand out from, the general body of men. Such men will obtain ever increasing joy in Jehovah (<hi type="italic">yâsaph</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Isa.37.31">Isa 37:31</reference>). Such a people of God would take the place of the oppressors (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.28.12">Isa 28:12</reference>) and scoffers (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.28.14">Isa 28:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.22">Isa 28:22</reference>), and those who thought evil (<hi type="italic">shâqad</hi>, <hi type="italic">invigilare</hi>, <hi type="italic">sedulo agere</hi>), i.e., the wretched planners, who made a חטא of every one who did not enter into their plans (i.e., who called him a <hi type="italic">chōtē'</hi>; cf., <reference osisRef="Deut.24.4">Deu 24:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.5">Ecc 5:5</reference>), and went to law with the man who openly opposed them in the gate (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.10">Amo 5:10</reference>; <hi type="italic">yeqōshūn</hi>, possibly the <hi type="italic">perf. kal</hi>, cf., <reference osisRef="Jer.50.24">Jer 50:24</reference>; according to the syntax, however, it is the <hi type="italic">fut. kal</hi> of <hi type="italic">qūsh</hi> = <hi type="italic">yâqōsh</hi>: see at <reference osisRef="Isa.26.16">Isa 26:16</reference>; Ges. §44, Anm. 4), and thrust away the righteous, i.e., forced him away from his just rights (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.2">Isa 10:2</reference>), by <hi type="italic">tōhū</hi>, i.e., accusations and pretences of the utmost worthlessness; for these would all have been swept away. This is the true explanation of the last clause, as given in the Targum, and not “into the desert and desolation,” as Knobel and Luzzatto suppose; for with Isaiah <hi type="italic">tōhū</hi> is the synonym for all such words as signify nothingness, groundlessness, and fraud. The prophet no doubt had in his mind, at the time that he uttered these words, the conduct of the people towards himself and his fellow-prophets, and such as were like-minded with them. The charge brought against him of being a conspirator, or a traitor to his country, was a <hi type="italic">tōhū</hi> of this kind. All these conspirators and persecutors Jehovah would clear entirely away.
entries.b3ad6abdf297424ab97e0360f1484cdd8f950a18: <reference osisRef="Isa.29.22-Isa.29.24">Isa 29:22-24</reference> <div eID="gen13184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13185" type="x-p"/> Everything that was incorrigible would be given up to destruction; and therefore the people of God, when it came out of the judgment, would have nothing of the same kind to look for again. <hi type="italic">“Therefore thus saith Jehovah of the house of Jacob, He who redeemed Abraham: Jacob shall not henceforth be ashamed, nor shall his face turn pale any more. For when he, when his children see the work of my hands in the midst of him, they will sanctify my name, and sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and shudder before the God of Israel. And those who were of an erring spirit discern understanding, and murmurers accept instruction.”</hi> With אל (for which Luzzatto, following Lowth, reads אל sda, “the God of the house of Jacob”) the theme is introduced to which the following utterance refers. The end of Israel will correspond to the holy root of its origin. Just as Abraham was separated from the human race that was sunk in heathenism, to become the ancestor of a nation of Jehovah, so would a remnant be separated from the great mass of Israel that was sunk in apostasy from Jehovah; and this remnant would be the foundation of a holy community well pleasing to God. And this would never be confounded or become pale with shame again (on <hi type="italic">bōsh</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Isa.1.29">Isa 1:29</reference>; <hi type="italic">châvar</hi> is a poetical Aramaism); for both sins and sinners that called forth the punishments of God, which had put them to shame, would have been swept away (cf., Zep 3:11). In the presence of this decisive work of punishment (<hi type="italic">ma‛ăseh</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.21">Isa 28:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.12">Isa 10:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">Isa 5:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.19">Isa 5:19</reference>), which Jehovah would perform in the heart of Israel, Israel itself would undergo a thorough change. ילדיו is in apposition to the subject in בּראתו, “when he, namely his children” (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.29.3">Job 29:3</reference>); and the expression “his children” is intentionally chosen instead of “his sons” (<hi type="italic">bânı̄m</hi>), to indicate that there would be a new generation, which would become, in the face of the judicial self-manifestation of Jehovah, a holy church, sanctifying Him, the Holy One of Israel. <hi type="italic">Yaqdı̄shū</hi> is continued in <hi type="italic">vehiqdı̄shū</hi>: the prophet intentionally repeats this most significant word, and <hi type="italic">he‛ĕrı̄ts</hi> is the parallel word to it, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.8.12">Isa 8:12</reference>-13. The new church would indeed not be a sinless one, or thoroughly perfect; but, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.29.24">Isa 29:24</reference>, the previous self-hardening in error would have been exchanged for a willing and living appropriation of right understanding, and the former murmuring resistance to the admonitions of Jehovah would have given place to a joyful and receptive thirst for instruction. There is the same interchange of <hi type="italic">Jacob</hi> and <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> here which we so frequently met with in chapters 40ff. And, in fact, throughout this undisputedly genuine prophecy of Isaiah, we can detect the language of chapters 40-66. Through the whole of the first part, indeed, we may trace the gradual development of the thoughts and forms which predominate there.  <chapter eID="Isa.29"/> <div eID="gen13185" type="x-p"/>

entries.26067faa4d6aa34415a60fb6b9619f571deaf8b2: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.29.1" sID="gen45117" type="section"/> <div sID="gen45118" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1. </hi>This appears to be another discourse, in which Isaiah threatens the city of Jerusalem. He calls it “Altar,” <note n="251"> <div sID="gen45119" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il l’appelle <hi type="italic">Ariel</hi>, c’est à dire, autel de Dieu</foreign>;” — “He calls it <hi type="italic">Ariel</hi>, that is, Altar of God.”<div eID="gen45119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45120" type="x-p"/> FT509 “Some, with the Chaldee, suppose it to be taken from the hearth of the great altar of burnt-offerings, which Ezekiel plainly calls by the same name; and that Jerusalem is here considered as the seat of the fire of God, la <foreign xml:lang="he">אור אל</foreign> (ō<hi type="italic">r ēl</hi>,) which should issue from thence to consume his enemies. Compare chap. <reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.31.9">Isaiah 31:9</reference>. Some, according to the common derivation of the word, <foreign xml:lang="he">ארי אל</foreign> (ă<hi type="italic">rīēl</hi>,) the lion of God, or the strong lion, suppose it to signify the strength of the place, by which it was enabled to resist and overcome all its enemies.” — <hi type="italic">Lowth</hi>. “Jonathan interprets it the altar of the Lord, and Ezekiel also (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ezek.43.15">Ezekiel 43:15</reference>) gives it this name. It is so called, on account of the fire of God, which couched like <foreign xml:lang="he">ארי</foreign> (ă<hi type="italic">rī</hi>,) a lion on the altar. Our Rabbins explain <foreign xml:lang="he">אריאל</foreign> (ă<hi type="italic">rīēl</hi>) to denote the temple of Jerusalem, which was narrow behind, and broad in front.” — <hi type="italic">Jarchi</hi>. “The greater part of interpreters are agreed, that <foreign xml:lang="he">אריאל</foreign> (ă<hi type="italic">rīēl</hi>) compounded of <foreign xml:lang="he">ארי</foreign> (ă<hi type="italic">rī</hi>) and <foreign xml:lang="he">אל</foreign> (ē<hi type="italic">l</hi>,) denotes the lion of God, or, as Castalio renders it, The Lion — God. But they differ in explaining the application of this name to Jerusalem.” — <hi type="italic">Rosenmüller</hi>. “The meaning of the Prophet, in my opinion, is, that ‘God will make Jerusalem the heart of his anger, which shall consume not only the enemies but the obstinate rebellious Jews.’ This meaning is elegant and emphatic, and agrees well with the wisdom of the prophet Isaiah. Ariel is here taken, in its true signification, not for the altar, but for the hearth of the altar, as in Ezekiel. The import of the name lies here. The hearth of the altar sustained the symbol of the most holy and pure will of God, by which all the sacrifices offered to God must be tried; and to this applies the justice of God, burning like a fire, and consuming the sinner, if no atonement be found. Jerusalem would become the theater of the divine judgments.” — <hi type="italic">Vitringa</hi>. “Isaiah foresees that the city will, in a short time, be besieged by a very numerous army of the Assyrians, and will be reduced to straits, and yet will not be vanquished by those multitudes, but, like a lion, will rise by divine power out of the severest encounters.” — <hi type="italic">Doederlein</hi><div eID="gen45120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45121" type="x-p"/> FT510 Instead of “Let them kill sacrifices,” Vitringa’s rendering, in which he has been followed by Lowth, Stock, and Alexander, is, “Let the feasts revolve.” — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen45121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45122" type="x-p"/> FT511 Symmachus, on whom Montfaucon bestows the exaggerated commendation of having adhered closely to the Hebrew text, wherever it differed from the Septuagint, renders the clause, <foreign xml:lang="el">καὶ ἐσταὶ κατώδυνος καὶ ὀδυνωμένη</foreign>, which has been closely followed by Jerome’s version, “<foreign xml:lang="la">Et erit tristis ac moerens</foreign>;” — “And she shall be sad and sorrowful.” — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen45122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45123" type="x-p"/> FT512 In both cases there are two synonyms, <foreign xml:lang="he">תאניה ואניה</foreign> (<hi type="italic">thăănīāh văănīāh</hi>,) which are derived from the same root. This peculiarity is imitated by the version of Symmachus quoted above, <foreign xml:lang="el">κατώδυνος καὶ ὀδυνωμένη</foreign>, and by that of Vitringa, (“<foreign xml:lang="la">mœstitia et mœror</foreign>,”) who remarks: “It is somewhat unusual to bring together words of the same termination and derived from the same root, but in this instance it produces an agreeable echo, which convinces me that it must have been frequently employed in poetical writings.” — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen45123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45124" type="x-p"/> FT513 “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que les ennemis feront en Jerusalem</foreign>;” — “Which the enemies shall make in Jerusalem.”<div eID="gen45124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45125" type="x-p"/> FT514 “Like a circle of tents. <foreign xml:lang="he">נדור</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">kăddūr</hi>,) like a <hi type="italic">Dowar</hi>; so the Arabs call a circular village of tents, such as they still live in.” — <hi type="italic">Stock</hi><div eID="gen45125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45126" type="x-p"/> FT515 “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qu’ils parleront bas, et comme du creux de la terre</foreign>;” — “That they will speak low, and as out of the heart of the earth.”<div eID="gen45126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45127" type="x-p"/> FT516 “And from the dust thou shalt chirp thy words, or, utter a feeble, stridulous sound, such as the vulgar supposed to be the voice of a ghost. This sound was imitated by necromancers, who had also the art of pitching their voice in such a manner as to make it appear to proceed out of the ground, or from what place they chose.” — <hi type="italic">Stock</hi><div eID="gen45127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45128" type="x-p"/> FT517 The Septuagint renders it, <foreign xml:lang="el">καὶ ἔσται ὡς κονιορτὸς ἀπὸ τροχοὺ ὁ πλοῦτος τῶν ἀσεβῶν</foreign>, “and as the small dust from the wheel shall be the multitude of the wicked.” Here it is necessary to attend to the distinction between <foreign xml:lang="el">τρόχος</foreign> and <foreign xml:lang="el">τροχὸς</foreign> — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen45128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45129" type="x-p"/> FT518 The military forces of Sennacherib, which shall be fuel for the fire, and shall be reduced to powder.” — <hi type="italic">Jarchi</hi><div eID="gen45129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45130" type="x-p"/> FT519 “They shall be destroyed by the pestilential blast <hi type="italic">Simoom</hi>, whose effects are instantaneous. Thevenot describes this wind with all the circumstances here enumerated, with thunder and lightning, insufferable heat, and a whirlwind of sand. By such an ‘angel of Jehovah,’ as it is called below, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.37.36">Isaiah 37:36</reference>,) was the host of Assyria destroyed.” — <hi type="italic">Stock</hi><div eID="gen45130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45131" type="x-p"/> FT520 “As a dream, when one thinks that he sees, and yet does not in reality see, so shall be the multitude of nations; they will indeed think that they are subduing the city of Jerusalem, but they shall be disappointed of that hope, they shall not succeed in it.” — <hi type="italic">Jarchi</hi><div eID="gen45131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45132" type="x-p"/> FT521 The comparison is elegant and beautiful in the highest degree, well wrought up, and perfectly suited to the end proposed: the image is extremely natural, but not obvious; it appeals to our inward feelings, not to our outward senses, and is applied to an event in its concomitant circumstances exactly similar, but in its nature totally different. For beauty and ingenuity it may fairly come in competition with one of the most elegant of Virgil, (greatly improved from Homer, Iliad, 22:199,) where he has applied to a different purpose, but not so happily, the same image of the ineffectual working of imagination in a dream. Virg. Æn. 12:908. Lucretius expresses the very same image with Isaiah, (iv. 1091.)” — <hi type="italic">Lowth</hi><div eID="gen45132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45133" type="x-p"/> FT522 “Cry ye out, and cry, <hi type="italic">or</hi>, Take your pleasure and riot.” — Eng. Ver. “Turn yourselves and stare around.” — <hi type="italic">Stock</hi>. Lowth’s rendering resembles this, but is somewhat paraphrastic, “They stare with a look of stupid surprise.” Professor Alexander’s comes nearer that of Calvin, “Be merry and blind!” — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen45133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45134" type="x-p"/> FT523 “Your prophets, and your rulers (Heb. heads).” — Eng. Ver. Our translators very correctly state that the literal meaning of <foreign xml:lang="he">רשיכם</foreign> (<hi type="italic">rāshēchĕm</hi>) is, “your heads.” Calvin treats it as an adjective, “your principal seers.” — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen45134" type="x-p"/> </note> because the chief defense of the city was in the “Altar;” <note n="252"> <div sID="gen45135" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen45135" type="x-p"/> </note> for although the citizens relied on other bulwarks, of which they had great abundance, still they placed more reliance on the Temple (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.7.4">Jeremiah 7:4</reference>) and the altar than on the other defences. While they thought that they were invincible in power and resources, they considered their strongest and most invincible fortress to consist in their being defended by the protection of God. They concluded that God was with them, so long as they enjoyed the altar and the sacrifices. Some think that the temple is here called “Ariel,” from the resemblance which it bore to the shape of a lion, being broader in front and narrower behind; but I think it better to take it simply as denoting “the Altar,” since Ezekiel also (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ezek.43.15">Ezekiel 43:15</reference>) gives it this name. This prediction is indeed directed against the whole city, but we must look at the design of the Prophet; for he intended to strip the Jews of their foolish confidence in imagining that God would assist them, so long as the altar and the sacrifices could remain, in which they falsely gloried, and thought that they had fully discharged their duty, though their conduct was base and detestable.<div eID="gen45118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45136" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The city where David dwelt.</hi> He now proceeds to the city, which he dignifies with the commendation of its high rank, on the ground of having been formerly inhabited by David, but intending, by this admission, to scatter the smoke of their vanity. Some understand by it the lesser Jerusalem, that is, the inner city, which also was surrounded by a wall; for there was a sort of two-fold Jerusalem, because it had increased, and had extended its walls beyond where they originally stood; but I think that this passage must be understood to relate to the whole city. He mentions <hi type="italic">David</hi>, because they gloried in his name, and boasted that the blessing of God continually dwelt in his palace; for the Lord had promised that “the kingdom of David would be for ever.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Sam.7.13">2 Samuel 7:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.89.37">Psalm 89:37</reference>.)<div eID="gen45136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45137" type="x-p"/>Hence we may infer how absurdly the Papists, in the present day, consider the Church to be bound to Peter’s chair, as if God could nowhere find a habitation in the whole world but in the See of Rome. We do not now dispute whether Peter was Bishop of the Church of Rome or not; but though we should admit that this is fully proved, was any promise made to Rome such as was made to Jerusalem? “This is my rest for ever: here will I dwell, for I have chosen it.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.132.14">Psalm 132:14</reference>.) And if even this were granted, do not we see what Isaiah declares about Jerusalem? That God is driven from it, when there is no room for doctrine, when the worship of God is corrupted. What then shall be said of Rome, which has no testimony? Can she boast of anything in preference to Jerusalem? If God pronounces a curse on the most holy city, which he had chosen in an especial manner, what must we say of the rest, who have overturned his holy laws and all godly institutions.<div eID="gen45137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45138" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Add year to year.</hi> This was added by the Prophet, because the Jews thought that they had escaped punishment, when any delay was granted to them. Wicked men think that God has made a truce with them, when they see no destruction close at hand; and therefore they promise to themselves unceasing prosperity, so long as the Lord permits them to enjoy peace and quietness. In opposition to this assurance of their safety the Prophet threatens that, though they continue to “offer sacrifices,” <note n="253"> <div sID="gen45139" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen45139" type="x-p"/> </note> and though they renew them year by year, still the Lord will execute his vengeance. We ought to learn from this, that, when the Lord delays to punish and to take vengeance, we ought not, on that account, to seize the occasion for delaying our repentance; for although he spares and bears with us for a time, our sin is not therefore blotted out, nor have we any reason to promise that we shall make a truce with him. Let us not then abuse his patience, but let us be more eager to obtain pardon.<div eID="gen45138" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen45117" osisID="Isa.29.1" type="section"/>
entries.a3463ebdc24d856767f893beef5ccf16757954e4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.29.2" sID="gen45140" type="section"/> <div sID="gen45141" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> <hi type="italic">But I will bring Ariel into distress</hi>. I think that <foreign xml:lang="he">ו</foreign> (<hi type="italic">vau</hi>) should here be taken for a disjunctive conjunction: “And yet I will execute my judgments and take vengeance, though, by delaying them for a time, it may seem as if I had forgiven.” He next threatens that he will give them <hi type="italic">grief</hi> and <hi type="italic">mourning</hi>, instead of the joy of the festivals. <foreign xml:lang="he">אניה</foreign> (ă<hi type="italic">nīāh</hi>) is viewed by some as an adjective, <note n="254"> <div sID="gen45142" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen45142" type="x-p"/> </note> but improperly; for it is used in the same manner by Jeremiah. <note n="255"> <div sID="gen45143" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen45143" type="x-p"/> </note> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Lam.2.5">Lamentations 2:5</reference>.) He declares that the Lord will reduce that city to straits, that the Jews might know that they had to contend with God, and not with men, and that, though the war was carried on by the Assyrians, still they might perceive that God was their leader.<div eID="gen45141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45144" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And it shall be to me as Ariel.</hi> This clause would not apply to the Temple alone; for he means that everything shall be made bloody by the slaughter which shall take place at Jerusalem; <note n="256"> <div sID="gen45145" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen45145" type="x-p"/> </note> and therefore he compares it to an “Altar,” on which victims of all kinds are slain, in the same manner as wicked men destined for slaughter are frequently compared to a sacrifice. In short, by alluding here to the word “Altar,” he says, that the whole city shall be “as Ariel,” because it shall overflow with the blood of the slain. Hence it is evident that the outward profession of worship, ceremonies, and the outward demonstrations of the favor of God, are of no avail, unless we sincerely obey him. By an ironical expression he tells hypocrites, (who with an impure heart present sacrifices of beasts to God, as if they were the offerings fitted to appease his anger,) that their labor is fruitless, and that, since they had profaned the Temple and the Altar, it was impossible to offer a proper sacrifice to God without slaying victims throughout the whole city, as if he had said, “There will be carnage in every part.” He makes use of the word “Sacrifice” figuratively, to denote the violent slaughter of those who refused to offer themselves willingly to God.<div eID="gen45144" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen45140" osisID="Isa.29.2" type="section"/>
entries.2f629d245da695bc7702d088ed14fcb1c6e3e123: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.29.3" sID="gen45146" type="section"/> <div sID="gen45147" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> <hi type="italic">And I will camp against thee round about.</hi> By the word <foreign xml:lang="he">כדור</foreign> (<hi type="italic">kāddūr</hi>) <note n="257"> <div sID="gen45148" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen45148" type="x-p"/> </note> he alludes to the roundness of a ball; and the expression corresponds to one commonly used, (“<foreign xml:lang="fr">Je l’environneray</foreign>,”) “I shall surround it.” Thus he shews that all means of escape will be cut off.<div eID="gen45147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45149" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And will lay siege against thee.</hi> This alludes to another method of invading the city; for either attacks are made at various points, or there is a regular siege. He confirms the doctrine of the former verse, and shews that this war will be carried on under God’s direction, and that the Assyrians, though they are hurried on by their passions and by the lust of power, will undertake nothing but by the command of God. He reckoned it to be of great importance to carry full conviction to the minds of the Jews, that all the evils which befell them were sent by God, that they might thus be led to enter into an examination of their crimes. As this doctrine is often found in the Scriptures, it ought to be the more carefully impressed on our minds; for it is not without good reason that it is so frequently repeated and inculcated by the Holy Spirit.<div eID="gen45149" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen45146" osisID="Isa.29.3" type="section"/>
entries.018bcbd6e349844ef3b13d45b76b981e46588cc0: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.29.4" sID="gen45150" type="section"/> <div sID="gen45151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.</hi> <hi type="italic">Then shalt thou be laid low.</hi> He describes scornfully that arrogance which led the Jews to despise all threatenings and admonitions, so long as they enjoyed prosperity, as is customary with all hypocrites. He says therefore, that, when their pride has been laid aside, they will afterwards be more submissive; not that they will change their dispositions, but because shame will restrain that wantonness in which they formerly indulged. We ought therefore to supply here an implied contrast. He addresses those who were puffed up by ambition, carried their heads high, and despised every one, as if they had not even been subject to God; for they ventured to curse and insult God himself, and to mock at his holy word. “This pride,” says Isaiah, “shall be laid low, and this arrogance shall cease.”<div eID="gen45151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45152" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And thy voice shall be out of the ground.</hi> <note n="258"> <div sID="gen45153" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen45153" type="x-p"/> </note> What he had formerly said he expresses more fully by a metaphor, that they will utter a low and confused noise as out of caverns. <note n="259"> <div sID="gen45154" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen45154" type="x-p"/> </note> The voice of those who formerly were so haughty and fierce is compared by him to the speech <hi type="italic">of soothsayers</hi>, who, in giving forth their oracles out of some deep and dark cave under ground, uttered some sort of confused muttering; for they did not speak articulately, but whispered. He declares that these boasters (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἀλάζονες</foreign>) shall resemble them. Some interpret this expression as if the Prophet meant that they will derive no benefit from the chastisement; but the words do not convey this meaning, and he afterwards says that the Jews will be brought to repentance. Yet he first strikes terror, in order to repress their insolence; for they arrogantly and rebelliously scorned all the threatenings of the Prophet. By their being “brought down,” therefore, he means nothing else than that they shall be covered with disgrace, so that they will not dare to utter, as from a lofty place, their proud and idle boastings.<div eID="gen45152" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.4" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen45150" osisID="Isa.29.4" type="section"/>
entries.f9b995a1f72b1e95b84c96045107d0d84cd5aa55: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.5" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.29.5" sID="gen45155" type="section"/> <div sID="gen45156" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">5.</hi> <hi type="italic">And as the small dust.</hi> <note n="260"> <div sID="gen45157" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen45157" type="x-p"/> </note> I shall first state the opinions of others, and afterwards I shall bring forward what I consider to be more probable. Almost all the commentators think that this expression denotes the enemies of the Jews; for they consider “foreigners” to mean “enemies,” and allege that the multitude of those who shall oppress the Jews shall be “like dust;” that is, it shall be innumerable. But when I examine closely the whole passage, I am more disposed to adopt a contrary opinion. I think that the Prophet speaks contemptuously of the garrisons on which the Jews foolishly relied, for they had in their pay foreign soldiers who were strong men.<div eID="gen45156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45158" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The multitude of the mighty ones.</hi> Such is the interpretation which I give to <foreign xml:lang="he">עריצים</foreign> (<hi type="italic">gnărītzīm</hi>), which is also its literal meaning; and I see no reason why some of the Jews should suppose it to mean ungodly or wicked persons. Since, therefore, the Jews brought various garrisons from a distance, they thought that they were well defended, and dreaded no danger. The Prophet threatens that their subsidiary troops, though they were a vast multitude, shall in vain create a disturbance, for they shall be like “dust” or “chaff,” that is, useless refuse, for they shall produce no effect. <note n="261"> <div sID="gen45159" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen45159" type="x-p"/> </note> Hence we ought to infer, that our wealth and resources, however great they are, shall be reduced to nothing, as soon as the Lord shall determine to deal with us as he has a right to do. The assistance of men lasts indeed for a time; but when the Lord shall lift up his hand in earnest, their strength must crumble down, and they must become like chaff.<div eID="gen45158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45160" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And it shall be in a moment suddenly.</hi> Some explain the concluding clause of this verse to mean, that the noise of the enemies’ attack shall spring up suddenly, and, as it were, in a moment. But I consider <foreign xml:lang="he">והיח</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">vĕhāyāh</hi>,) <hi type="italic">and it shall be</hi>, to relate to the time of duration, which he declares will be momentary; that is, those military aids shall not last long, but shall quickly vanish away. <note n="262"> <div sID="gen45161" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen45161" type="x-p"/> </note> In vain do men boast of them, for God is their enemy.<div eID="gen45160" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.5" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen45155" osisID="Isa.29.5" type="section"/>
entries.39c1ba3473094476ebec5f31b11d1fb281b88ed0: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.6" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.29.6" sID="gen45162" type="section"/> <div sID="gen45163" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6.</hi> <hi type="italic">From Jehovah of hosts shalt thou be visited.</hi> He next assigns the reason why all this multitude of garrisons shall be “like chaff;” and he expresses this by an opposite metaphor, for with those soldiers he contrasts the anger and “visitation of the Lord.” What is “chaff” to the flame of “a devouring fire?” What is “dust” to the force and violence of a “whirlwind?” He shews that the vengeance of God will be such as all their preparations shall be unable to resist. This meaning, in my opinion, makes the passage to flow easily, and the clauses will not be so well adjusted, if we follow a different interpretation.<div eID="gen45163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45164" type="x-p"/>Hence we learn that those who assail us can do no more than what the Lord permits them to do. If therefore the Lord determine to save us, the enemies will accomplish nothing, though they raise up the whole world against us. On the other hand, if he determine to chastise us, we shall not be able to ward off his wrath by any force or bulwarks, which shall quickly be thrown down as by a “whirlwind,” and shall even be consumed as by “a flame.”<div eID="gen45164" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.6" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen45162" osisID="Isa.29.6" type="section"/>
entries.fc925bedf4bcf6ecf569a5312e9b9ce4f4ab2969: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.7" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.29.7" sID="gen45165" type="section"/> <div sID="gen45166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7.</hi> <hi type="italic">As a dream of a night-vision.</hi> This verse also I interpret differently from others; for they think that the Prophet intended to bring consolation to the godly. There is undoubtedly great plausibility in this view, and it contains an excellent doctrine, namely, that the enemies of the Church resemble “dreamers” in this respect, that the Lord disappoints their hopes, even when they think that they have almost gained their object. <note n="263"> <div sID="gen45167" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen45167" type="x-p"/> </note> But this interpretation does not appear to me to agree well with the text. Sometimes it happens that, when a sentence is beautiful, it attracts us to it, and causes us to steal away from the true meaning, so that we do not adhere closely to the context, or spend much time in investigating the author’s meaning. Let us therefore inquire if this be the true meaning of the Prophet.<div eID="gen45166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45168" type="x-p"/>Since he afterwards proceeds again to utter threatenings, I have no doubt that here he follows out the same subject, which otherwise would be improperly broken off by the present statement. He censures the Jews, and rebukes them for their obstinacy, in boldly despising God and all his threatenings. In short, by a most appropriate metaphor, he reproves them for their false confidence and presumption, when he threatens that the enemies shall arrive suddenly and unexpectedly, while the Jews shall imagine that they are enjoying profound peace, and are very far from all danger; and that the event shall be so sudden and unexpected, that it will appear to be “a dream.” “Although then,” says he, “thou indulgest the hope of uninterrupted repose, the Lord will quickly awake thee, and will drive away thy presumption.”<div eID="gen45168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45169" type="x-p"/>The Prophet says wittily, that the Jews are “dreaming,” because, in consequence of being drowned in their pleasures, they neither see nor feel anything, but, amidst the dizzy whirl, stupidly fancy that they are happy. Hence he infers that the enemies will come, as in “a dream,” to strike terror into those who are asleep, as it frequently happens that a pleasant and delightful sleep is disturbed by frightful dreams. It follows from this, that the pleasures which have lulled them to sleep will be of no advantage to them; for, though they do not at all think of it, yet a tumult will arise suddenly. This might still have been somewhat obscure, if he had not explained the subject more fully in the following verse.<div eID="gen45169" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen45165" osisID="Isa.29.7" type="section"/>
entries.a7d282f2eb0319c20b751a8829e84db703b73cfa: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.8" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.29.8" sID="gen45170" type="section"/> <div sID="gen45171" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8.</hi> <hi type="italic">It shall be therefore as when a hungry man dreameth.</hi> He compares the Jews to “hungry men,” who are indeed asleep, but whose empty stomach craves for food; for it is natural for men to dream about food and entertainments when they are in want of them. Thus, while the Jews watched, they were like “hungry men.” The Lord continually warned them by his prophets, and invited them to the divine feasts of the word; but they despised those feasts, and chose rather to take refuge wholly in their vices, and to fall asleep in them, than to partake fully of those sacred feasts. Accordingly, while they quieted their consciences, they imagined that they had abundance of all things, and that they were free from every inconvenience. Isaiah declares that they greatly resemble this “dream” and airy “vision;” for, when they have been aroused by a sudden calamity, they shall feel how empty and insubstantial those “dreams and visions” were, and how false and delusive was the opinion which they had formed that they enjoyed abundance. As “hungry men,” who have had such dreams, are rendered more feeble by them, so the people, who had been falsely persuaded that everything was going on well with them, will endure much greater uneasiness than if they had never cherished in their minds such a thought, but, on the contrary, had been aware of their poverty and nakedness.<div eID="gen45171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45172" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">So shall be the multitude.</hi> At first sight, the expression appears to be harsh, when he says, “The multitude of those who fight against Ariel shall be as a dream;” but it ought to be explained in this manner: — “When the Jews, through false hope, shall promise to themselves deliverance, as if the enemies would be driven far away, they shall quickly feel that they had been deceived; in the same manner as a person whom hunger leads to dream that he is feasting luxuriously, as soon as he awakes, feels that his hunger is keener than before.” I see nothing here, therefore, that is fitted to yield consolation, for the Prophet pursues the same subject, and exclaims against the scorn and rebellion of the Jews, on whom the Prophet could make no impression by exhortation or threatenings. <note n="264"> <div sID="gen45173" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen45173" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen45172" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.8" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen45170" osisID="Isa.29.8" type="section"/>
entries.294e57f0f50d86dfa4ad2bd09df0e88b3dca117c: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.29.9" sID="gen45174" type="section"/> <div sID="gen45175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9.</hi> <hi type="italic">Tarry and wonder. </hi>Isaiah follows out the same subject, and attacks more keenly the gross stupidity of the people. Instead of “tarry,” some render the term, “Be amazed;” but the view which I prefer may be thus expressed: “Though they dwell much and long on this thought, yet it will end in nothing else than that, by long continued thought, their minds shall be amazed.” In short, he means that the judgment of God will so completely overwhelm their minds, that though they torture themselves by thinking and reflecting, still they will be unable to find any outlet or conclusion.<div eID="gen45175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45176" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">They are drunken, and not with wine.</hi> He now assigns the reason why fixed thought does not aid them in conquering their slowness of apprehension. It is, because they resemble <hi type="italic">drunkards</hi>. When, therefore, they neither see nor understand anything in the works of God, he shews that this is owing to their indolence and stupidity. A proof of this is given daily in many persons; for spiritual “drunkenness” engrosses and stupefies all their senses to such a degree, that they are blind to the plainest subjects; and, when God shews the brightest light of justice and equity, they are so completely dazzled, that their dim vision bewilders them more and more. This stupidity is a just punishment which the Lord inflicts on them on account of their unbelief.<div eID="gen45176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45177" type="x-p"/>In order that we may apply this statement of the Prophet for our own use, it is proper to observe, that these words of the Prophet must not be understood to be commands, as if he enjoined them to stop and think longer; but, on the contrary, he mocks and reproves their stupidity, as we have already said. (<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pensez y tant que vous voudrez, vous n’y entendres rien</foreign>) “Think as much as you please about it, you will not at all understand it.”<div eID="gen45177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45178" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">They are blinded, and they blind.</hi> <note n="265"> <div sID="gen45179" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen45179" type="x-p"/> </note> He means, that they are destitute of judgment and understanding, and that consequently it is useless for them to contemplate these works of God; for as the brightness of the sun is of no avail to the toad, so a blinded understanding in vain does its utmost to comprehend the majestic works of God. When he says that “they are blinded,” he means that by nature we are created so as to be endued with reason and understanding for contemplating the works of God; that our being “blinded” is, so to speak, an accidental fault, and that the drunkenness does not naturally belong to us, for it is owing to the ingratitude of men, which the Lord justly censures.<div eID="gen45178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45180" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">They stagger.</hi> This “staggering” of the mind is contrasted by him with a calm and quiet exercise of reason; for he means that violence of the passions which agitates the mind, and causes it to waver and reel.<div eID="gen45180" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.9" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen45174" osisID="Isa.29.9" type="section"/>
entries.26ddc6d5342c5fceff23ef9006eed84e91000cd2: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.29.10" sID="gen45181" type="section"/> <div sID="gen45182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10.</hi> <hi type="italic">Because Jehovah hath overpowered you with the spirit of slumber.</hi> For the purpose of shewing more clearly the source of this blindness, he attributes it to the judgment of God, who determined to punish in this manner the wickedness of the people. As it belongs to him to give eyes to see, and to enlighten minds by the spirit of judgment and understanding, so he alone deprives us of all light, when he sees that by a wicked and depraved hatred of the truth we of our own accord wish for darkness. Accordingly, when men are blind, and especially in things so plain and obvious, we perceive his righteous judgment.<div eID="gen45182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45183" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Your prophets and principal seers.</hi> <note n="266"> <div sID="gen45184" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen45184" type="x-p"/> </note> He adds, that the people are deprived of those aids and helps which ought to have imparted light to the understanding and given direction to others. <note n="267"> <div sID="gen45185" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et monstrer le chemin aux autres</foreign>;” — “And point out the way to others.”<div eID="gen45185" type="x-p"/> </note> Such was the office of the prophets, whom he describes by both of these names, <foreign xml:lang="he">נביאים</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">nēbīīm</hi>,) and <foreign xml:lang="he">חזים</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">chōzīm</hi>,) “prophets” and “seers.” In short, he means not only that men who are endued with reason and understanding will be deprived of common sense, but that their teachers also, whose duty it was to enlighten others, will be altogether senseless so as not to know the road, and, being covered with the darkness of ignorance, will shamefully go astray, and will be so far from directing others that they will not even be able to guide themselves.<div eID="gen45183" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen45181" osisID="Isa.29.10" type="section"/>
entries.cc87cc63433f274c6c3f5992d09b4a4bc7e1dcd7: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.29.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.29.11" sID="gen45186" type="section"/> <div sID="gen45187" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11.</hi> <hi type="italic">Therefore every vision hath become to you.</hi> The Prophet expresses still more clearly what he had formerly said, that the blindness of the Jews will be so great that, though the Lord enlightens them by the clearest light of his word, they will understand nothing.
